title: About this website
snippet: About CitizenGuide.KE — independent civic information, not an official government website.
content: Home About About CitizenGuide.KE CitizenGuide.KE is an independent directory of the Kenyan government. It brings together information about government institutions, leaders, laws and public services in one place. This is an independent website. It is not run, funded or endorsed by the Government of Kenya. Why we built this website Kenya's government includes many ministries, agencies, commissions and public bodies. Each runs its own website and keeps its own records. It can be difficult to find accurate information because: information is spread across many different websites names and acronyms can be confusing leaders and structures change frequently CitizenGuide.KE brings this information together so you can find what you need quickly. The problem we are solving Government information is often hard to find. Official records are spread across different department websites, and it can be difficult to know exactly what each agency does or where their offices are located. Many people want clearer information about how the government works, how money is spent, and how laws are made. We aim to make this information easy to find and understand. Where our information comes from We provide a clear and neutral directory of government institutions, public services and leaders. We only use information from official public sources. This includes: the Kenya Gazette parliamentary records (Hansard) court registries data from the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Keeping information up to date Government structures change. New ministries are created, leaders are appointed, and policies are updated. We review our information regularly and update it when official sources publish changes. However, there may be a short delay between an official announcement and our update. For the most current information, always check the official government website of the relevant institution. How this website is designed CitizenGuide.KE is a GDS-inspired civic information site for Kenya. We adapt open patterns from the UK Government Digital Service Design System (opens in a new tab) — plain language, clear structure and accessibility — with our own branding, colours and Kenyan content. We are not GOV.UK, not a Government of Kenya website, and not affiliated with the UK government. We use the design system's open components and ideas; we do not use the GOV.UK logo, crown or official brand. We use a clean layout with high contrast and simple navigation. This makes the website easier to read on any device and more usable with assistive technologies. Editorial standards We follow a published editorial policy : source hierarchy, plain language, independence from party politics, and how we handle updates. If you find an error, use our corrections process . Help us improve CitizenGuide.KE is a work in progress. We welcome your feedback and suggestions. If you find an error or have a suggestion, please get in touch: Give feedback Contact this website Request a correction Important notice CitizenGuide.KE is an informational directory only. We do not process applications, accept payments, or provide official government services. If you need to apply for a service, make a payment, or submit an official application, you must use the official government portals, such as the eCitizen portal or the specific ministry website. Read the full disclaimer . Related pages

title: Access to information
snippet: Your rights under the Access to Information Act.
content: Access to information How Kenyans can request information from public bodies under the Constitution and the Access to Information Act. Home Help Access to information Access to information Your right in brief protects access to information held by the State. It sits within . The Access to Information Act sets out procedures, timelines and exemptions in more detail — see Acts of Parliament . This page is a plain-language overview. It is not legal advice. Before you make a formal request Check whether the information is already published (websites, Gazette, open data portals, budget documents) Identify the public body that holds the information Be as specific as you can about what you need Our open data and documents pages may help for some civic datasets and policy papers. Making a request Requests are usually made in writing to the public entity that holds the information, following that entity’s published access to information procedures where available. Keep a copy of your request and any reference number. Public bodies should respond within the timelines set in law, or explain lawful reasons for delay, refusal or partial disclosure. If you are refused or ignored Review and appeal routes exist under the Act and related institutions. The Commission on Administrative Justice has a role in access to information oversight. Serious disputes may end up in court. Consider independent legal advice for complex cases. How to complain about government Limitations Not all information must be released. The law provides exemptions (for example certain national security, privacy or commercial confidentiality grounds). Bodies should cite the legal basis when refusing. Information on this website CitizenGuide.KE republishes and organises public information. A request for records we do not hold should go to the public body, not to us. To correct something we published, use corrections . title: Accessibility statement
snippet: Accessibility statement for CitizenGuide.KE, including our accessibility standards, known limitations, testing and how to report a problem.
content: Accessibility statement Accessibility statement for CitizenGuide.KE, including our accessibility standards, known limitations, testing and how to report a problem. Home Accessibility statement Accessibility statement for CitizenGuide.KE CitizenGuide.KE is an independent civic information platform. We design and improve the website with accessibility in mind and aim to meet WCAG 2.2 Level AA and align with Kenya Standard KS 2952. Using this website We want you to be able to use CitizenGuide.KE in the way that works best for you. We design the website so that you should be able to: change colours, contrast levels and fonts using your browser or device settings zoom in up to 400% without text becoming unreadable or requiring unnecessary horizontal scrolling navigate the website using a keyboard without relying on a mouse use speech recognition software to navigate and interact with the website use screen readers such as NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver understand links and controls from their accessible names and surrounding context use the website across different screen sizes and mobile devices We also aim to write content in plain language and use consistent headings, navigation and page structures. AbilityNet (opens in a new tab) has guidance on making your computer, phone or tablet easier to use if you have a disability. Accessibility standards we use Our accessibility work is guided primarily by: the Kenya Standard on Accessibility of ICT Products and Services (KS 2952) the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 Kenya Standard KS 2952 Kenya Standard KS 2952 sets accessibility requirements for ICT products and services, including considerations relevant to digital services used by people with disabilities. You can read the Kenya Standard on Accessibility of ICT Products and Services (PDF, opens in a new tab) . WCAG 2.2 We use Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 (opens in a new tab) as our main web accessibility benchmark and aim for Level AA. WCAG covers areas such as text alternatives, keyboard access, colour contrast, page structure, forms, focus behaviour and compatibility with assistive technologies. How accessible CitizenGuide.KE is We are continually reviewing CitizenGuide.KE against our accessibility targets. Most of the main website interface is designed with accessibility in mind, but we know that some content and features may not yet fully meet those targets. Known limitations include: some older PDF documents and historical public records may not be fully accessible to screen-reader users some source documents provided by external public bodies may have incomplete headings, tagging or text alternatives some complex tables may require horizontal scrolling on smaller screens updates to live search results or filters may not always be announced immediately by every screen reader accessibility of content on external websites linked from CitizenGuide.KE is outside our control If you find another accessibility problem, please tell us. Reports from users are an important part of how we identify and prioritise improvements. PDFs and source documents CitizenGuide.KE may link to or make available legislation, Gazette notices, reports and other documents originally published by government institutions or other public bodies. Some historical or third-party PDFs may not have been created with accessibility in mind. For example, a document may: contain scanned pages without accessible text have missing or incorrect document tags lack a logical heading structure contain tables that are difficult for screen readers to interpret lack appropriate text descriptions for informative images Where practical, we aim to provide accessible HTML information alongside important source documents or link users to an accessible version where one is available. If you cannot access information contained in a document, contact us and tell us which document or page you need. Live search, filters and dynamic content CitizenGuide.KE contains search tools, filters, tables and other interactive components for navigating large amounts of civic information. We aim to make changes in dynamic content understandable to assistive technologies, including by using appropriate focus management, semantic HTML and status messages where needed. Some live search or filtering updates may not yet be announced consistently by every combination of browser and screen reader. We are continuing to improve these components. External websites CitizenGuide.KE links to websites operated by government institutions, courts, Parliament, counties and other organisations. We do not control the accessibility of those external websites or documents. External links that open in a new tab are identified visually with an external-link symbol and include additional text for screen readers indicating that the link opens in a new tab. What we have done to improve accessibility CitizenGuide.KE uses accessible design patterns and semantic web technologies as the foundation of its interface. Our approach includes: using semantic HTML wherever possible maintaining a logical heading structure providing visible keyboard focus states supporting keyboard navigation designing text and interface elements with sufficient colour contrast providing alternative text for images that communicate information hiding purely decorative images from assistive technologies providing labels and instructions for form controls providing clear validation and error messages avoiding generic link text such as "click here" where a more descriptive link can be used supporting browser zoom and responsive layouts using accessible tables and responsive table containers where tabular information is necessary identifying external links that open in a new browser tab GOV.UK Frontend CitizenGuide.KE uses and adapts open-source components and patterns from GOV.UK Frontend and the GOV.UK Design System (opens in a new tab) as part of our accessibility foundation. CitizenGuide.KE has its own content, branding and identity. We are independent of the UK Government, Government Digital Service and the Government of Kenya. How we test accessibility We use a combination of automated and manual checks when reviewing the accessibility of CitizenGuide.KE. Our testing may include: automated accessibility checks using axe and Lighthouse keyboard-only navigation focus order and visible focus checks screen-reader testing using NVDA and VoiceOver colour-contrast checks browser zoom testing testing layouts at different viewport sizes reviewing semantic HTML and ARIA use reviewing forms, errors and validation messages Automated testing can identify many accessibility problems, but it cannot establish accessibility on its own. We therefore combine it with manual checks. Reporting an accessibility problem We are always looking to improve the accessibility of CitizenGuide.KE. If you find an accessibility problem, or if something on the website is difficult or impossible for you to use, contact CitizenGuide.KE . It helps if you tell us: the page or feature where you experienced the problem what you were trying to do what went wrong the browser, device or assistive technology you were using, if you know it We will consider the issue and use the information to help us investigate and improve the website. Requesting information in another format If you need information published on CitizenGuide.KE in a different accessible format, contact us and tell us what you need. This may include a request for: accessible HTML an accessible version of a PDF large-print text a simplified or easier-to-read explanation another reasonable accessible format Contact us about an accessible format . Contacting CitizenGuide.KE CitizenGuide.KE is primarily an online platform. The best way to contact us about an accessibility issue is through our contact page . You can also use our feedback service to tell us about problems with the website. Reviewing this statement We review this accessibility statement as CitizenGuide.KE develops, particularly when we introduce significant new interfaces or functionality. Accessibility testing is also part of our ongoing development and quality-assurance work. title: How to complain about government
snippet: Where to complain about public services, maladministration, corruption, police conduct, human rights violations, access to information and electoral issues in Kenya.
content: How to complain about government Where to complain about public services, maladministration, corruption, police conduct, human rights violations, access to information and electoral issues in Kenya. Home Help Complain about government How to complain about government CitizenGuide.KE cannot investigate a public body, order compensation, reverse an official decision or act as your lawyer. We can help you identify the institution that may handle your complaint. Choose the type of complaint Poor service, delay or unfair treatment Start with the public institution involved. If the matter is not resolved, the Commission on Administrative Justice may be able to consider it. Corruption or bribery Report suspected corruption to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC). Police misconduct Complaints about police conduct can be made to the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA). Human rights violation The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) receives complaints about alleged human rights violations. Information refused by a public body Follow the access to information process. The Commission on Administrative Justice oversees and enforces the Access to Information Act. Election complaint The correct route depends on whether the issue concerns voter registration, nomination, electoral conduct or a dispute after election results have been declared. Start with the organisation involved For many service complaints, start with the ministry, department, agency, commission or county government responsible for the service. This is particularly useful for issues such as: an application that has been delayed a payment that has not been reflected incorrect information given by an office a document that has not been issued a service that was not provided as expected a decision you want the institution to explain or review Use the institution's official complaints, customer care or review process where one exists. Find a government institution What to include in a complaint A clear complaint is easier for an institution to understand and investigate. Where relevant, include: your name and contact details the institution or office involved what happened the date and location application, receipt, case or reference numbers the names or positions of officers involved, if known copies of relevant documents or correspondence what you have already done to resolve the matter what outcome you are asking for Keep copies of complaints, receipts, emails, letters and reference numbers. Do not hand over original documents unless an official process specifically requires them. Poor administration or unfair treatment The Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ), also known as the Office of the Ombudsman, deals with maladministration in the public sector. Its mandate includes complaints involving matters such as: unreasonable delay abuse of power unfair treatment manifest injustice discourtesy by public officers The Commission's mandate extends to national and county government administration. Independent commissions are provided for under . Complain to the Commission on Administrative Justice You can also read about constitutional commissions . Access to information Article 35 of the Constitution protects the right of access to information in the circumstances provided by the Constitution. The Access to Information Act, 2016 provides procedures for exercising that right. The Commission on Administrative Justice oversees and enforces implementation of the Access to Information Act. If a request has been refused, ignored or otherwise not handled in accordance with the applicable process, see: How to request access to information Corruption and bribery Suspected corruption, bribery or economic crime can be reported to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC). EACC currently accepts reports through several channels, including in person, by telephone, in writing and through an anonymous reporting system. Report corruption to EACC Do not make an unofficial payment to someone who claims they can guarantee, accelerate or "unlock" a government service. Read scams and fake websites if the incident involves suspicious payments, impersonation or phishing. Complaints about the police The Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) provides independent civilian oversight of policing and receives complaints relating to police conduct within its mandate. Complaints may concern matters such as alleged misconduct, abuse of police powers or other conduct that falls within IPOA's legal mandate. Make or learn about a complaint to IPOA If somebody is in immediate danger or a crime is happening now, deal with the emergency first. See emergency and safety information . Human rights violations The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) receives complaints about alleged violations of human rights. Its complaint system can be relevant where a person believes that a right or fundamental freedom has been violated. Make a human rights complaint to KNCHR Serious criminal conduct should also be reported through the appropriate law-enforcement process. Elections and electoral disputes The correct route for an election complaint depends on what has happened and when. The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) handles electoral disputes within its constitutional and statutory mandate, including certain disputes relating to voter registration, nominations and electoral conduct. However, IEBC's dispute-resolution mandate does not extend to election petitions and disputes arising after the declaration of election results. Those matters may fall to the courts under the applicable election law. ! Warning Electoral complaints can have strict filing deadlines. Do not delay while relying only on general guidance. Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission You can also start from the CitizenGuide.KE elections hub . If the issue involves a political party Some disputes involving political parties fall under processes separate from IEBC, including the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal where the law gives it jurisdiction. The correct route depends on the type of dispute, the parties involved and the stage of the electoral process. If a legal deadline may apply, consider getting legal advice promptly. Going to court Some disputes cannot be resolved through an ordinary complaints process and may require review or determination by a court or tribunal. This may be particularly important where you are challenging: the legality of an administrative decision a decision affecting constitutional rights an election result a decision for which legislation provides a specific appeal a matter requiring an enforceable court order The Judiciary is independent. Court procedures, jurisdiction and filing deadlines depend on the type of case. Consider legal advice or legal aid where appropriate. CitizenGuide.KE does not provide legal representation. Crime, justice and the law If more than one institution may be involved A single incident can involve more than one issue. For example, an allegation about a police officer demanding a bribe could raise both police-conduct and corruption issues. A public institution refusing information could raise both an internal service complaint and an access-to-information issue. You do not need to force every problem into one category. Use the complaint route that matches each part of the issue and follow any referral instructions given by the responsible institution. If your complaint is not accepted An institution may decide that a complaint falls outside its legal mandate or that another process must be used. If this happens: ask for the reason where it is not already clear ask whether another institution or appeal route is appropriate keep the response and any reference number check whether there is a deadline for review, appeal or court action Complaints about CitizenGuide.KE CitizenGuide.KE is not a government institution. If your concern is about information published on this website, do not send the complaint to a government oversight body simply because the page is about government. If information on CitizenGuide.KE appears inaccurate, outdated or misleading, use our corrections process . For another issue concerning this website, contact CitizenGuide.KE . Before you submit a complaint Check that: you have identified the correct institution you have described what happened clearly important dates and reference numbers are included supporting evidence is organised you have said what outcome you are seeking you have checked for any complaint, appeal or filing deadline you are using the institution's genuine website or official contact channel Last updated: 10 September 2026 Access to information Contact government Commissions Emergency and safety Scams and fake websites Help and support

title: Content style guide
snippet: How CitizenGuide.KE writes and structures civic information using plain language, consistent terminology and accessible content design.
content: Content style guide How CitizenGuide.KE writes and structures civic information using plain language, consistent terminology and accessible content design. Home About Content style guide Content style guide CitizenGuide.KE is an independent civic information platform. This guide is inspired by established public-service content design practices, including GOV.UK patterns, but CitizenGuide.KE is not GOV.UK and is not a Government of Kenya website. Principles Page structure Headings and summaries Language and style Service pages Institutions and office holders Laws and legal material Links Dates, money and numbers Tables and structured data Sources and attribution Accessibility AI-assisted content Do not Review before publishing Principles Content should help someone understand a civic issue, identify the responsible institution or find the correct official source without having to understand the structure of government first. Start with the user need, not the organisation chart. Give each page one clear main purpose. Be accurate, neutral and politically independent. Prefer primary and authoritative sources. Use plain language without changing legal meaning. Make important dates, fees and limitations easy to find. Say when information can change or varies by county. Make it clear when users are leaving CitizenGuide.KE for an official service. Never imply that CitizenGuide.KE is a government department, official portal or government payment service. Our sourcing and verification rules are explained in the editorial policy . Page structure Use a predictable structure so users can quickly understand a page and find the information they need. A typical CitizenGuide.KE page should contain: breadcrumbs showing where the page sits one clear H1 a short lead explaining what the page helps the user do an independence, safety or scam warning where it is genuinely useful a contents list on longer pages H2 sections in the order users are likely to need them source or update information where relevant related internal links Do not add sections simply to make a page look complete. Every section should answer a likely user question. Headings and summaries Page titles Page titles should describe the subject or user task clearly. Avoid promotional wording, slogans and internal administrative terminology. For services, prefer a verb-led title where that accurately describes the task. For example: Use: Apply for a passport Avoid: Passport application services Lead paragraphs The lead should explain the value of the page in one or two sentences. Do not repeat the H1 word for word. Section headings Use descriptive headings that make sense when scanned on their own. Use: Who can apply Avoid: Eligibility information Use: How much it costs Avoid: Fees section Do not skip heading levels. An H3 should sit within an H2 section, not directly under the page title without a reason. Language and style Use Kenyan English for primary English-language content. Use active voice wherever it makes the sentence clearer. Address the reader as “you” when giving guidance. Prefer everyday words to formal administrative language. Keep sentences reasonably short. Keep paragraphs focused on one idea. Avoid marketing language, hype and superlatives. Avoid unnecessarily academic or legalistic wording. Keep necessary legal terms where simplifying them could change their meaning. Active voice Use: Apply through eCitizen. Avoid: Applications may be made through eCitizen. Acronyms Spell out an unfamiliar organisation or term the first time it appears, followed by the acronym in brackets if the acronym will be used again. For example: Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA). Do not expand an acronym repeatedly on the same page unless users may enter the page at a section where the context would otherwise be unclear. Capital letters Use capitals for proper names and official titles where appropriate. Do not capitalise ordinary concepts simply to make them appear important. Parliament of Kenya National Assembly Ministry of Health county government public service government services Kiswahili and other languages English is currently the primary language of CitizenGuide.KE. Kiswahili and other Kenyan-language versions may be introduced where appropriate. A translation should preserve the meaning of the source rather than translate administrative terminology literally where doing so makes the result unclear. Service pages Service pages help users understand what they need before they leave CitizenGuide.KE for an official service. Where relevant, include: a task-focused title the responsible institution who can use the service what the user needs before starting fees and charges processing times, if reliably sourced the official service link the date the information was checked or updated Start buttons Use one main Start button where a page has a clear official online service. The button must take the user to the real official service. Do not place a Start button on a page if there is no action for the user to start. Make it clear that the destination is external where the service is not operated by CitizenGuide.KE. Fees State the fee, what it covers and the date or source where possible. If charges may vary, say so instead of presenting one amount as universally applicable. Institutions and office holders Institution names Use the institution's official name on first reference. Use a recognised acronym afterwards where this makes the page easier to read. Avoid informal abbreviations that the institution itself does not use. Office holders Make clear whether a page is describing an office or the current person holding that office. Current office-holder information should be dated or regularly reviewed because appointments, elections, resignations and court decisions can change it. Use titles only where they help identify the person's official role. Avoid honorific inflation. Laws and legal material Legal material should be described accurately and without implying that a CitizenGuide.KE summary is the law itself. Legislation Use the official title of an Act on first reference. Include the year and chapter or citation where this is useful for identification. Distinguish clearly between: the Constitution an Act of Parliament a Bill regulations a Gazette notice a court judgment or ruling a policy or administrative guideline Do not describe a Bill as law before it has completed the necessary legislative process. Articles and sections Use the formal numbering of the source. For Constitution pages, internal links may use routes such as: /constitution/chapter/4/article/35 Link labels should give users meaningful context, for example: Article 35 — Access to information . Plain-language explanations Explain what a provision means in practical terms, but do not present an interpretation as the statutory text. Where exact wording matters, direct the user to the authoritative source. Links Internal links Link to relevant CitizenGuide.KE pages when they help the user understand the subject or continue their journey. Do not add internal links merely for search-engine optimisation. External links Use external links when the external destination is authoritative or materially useful to the user. Prefer the official source over a secondary copy where a usable official source exists. External links that open in a new tab should display the external link arrow and include hidden text for assistive technologies. Example: Kenya Law (opens in a new tab) Link text should describe the destination or action. Use: Read the Access to Information Act Avoid: Click here Avoid linking entire sentences unless the whole sentence is the meaningful link label. Dates, money and numbers Dates Use day, month, year without unnecessary punctuation. Use: 15 July 2026 Avoid: 15/07/26 Include a year where there is any reasonable chance of ambiguity. Use exact dates rather than relative wording such as "yesterday" on long-lived civic information pages. Money Use KSh for Kenyan shillings in ordinary CitizenGuide.KE prose. KSh 500 KSh 1,050 KSh 25,000 KSh 1.5 million where precision to the shilling is unnecessary Do not write Kshs , KES. or multiple different currency styles on the same page unless you are reproducing an official source exactly. Percentages Use numerals with the percentage sign where this is clearest: 10% . Large numbers Use commas to make large exact numbers easier to read: 1,250,000 . Tables and structured data Use a table when users need to compare values across rows and columns. Do not use a table merely to align ordinary text. Tables should: have meaningful column headings have an accessible caption where appropriate remain usable on smaller screens use consistent formats for dates, money and status values avoid unexplained abbreviations For large datasets, provide search, filtering or pagination when those tools genuinely help users find a record. Do not hide important explanatory information inside a table if it should instead appear in the surrounding page content. Sources and attribution Important factual claims should be traceable to reliable source material. Where appropriate, record: the source institution the document or publication title the date of the source the relevant Act, Gazette notice or record identifier a link to the authoritative online source the date the information was checked Do not make a source look more authoritative than it is. A social media post, news report and Gazette notice should not be labelled as though they carry the same evidential weight. Read the editorial policy for our source hierarchy. Accessibility Content should remain understandable and navigable when users rely on assistive technologies, keyboard navigation, zoom or smaller screens. Use headings in a logical order. Use descriptive link text. Do not communicate meaning through colour alone. Give informative images meaningful alternative text. Give decorative images empty alternative text. Use lists only when the information is genuinely a list. Use proper table headings for tabular information. Avoid unnecessarily long blocks of text. Identify links that open external websites in a new tab. Read our accessibility statement . AI-assisted content Artificial intelligence and other automated tools may assist with research organisation, drafting, summarisation, classification or identifying material for review. AI output must not be treated as a source. Before publishing factual civic information produced or assisted by an automated tool: verify factual claims against appropriate sources check names, dates, offices, fees and legal references check that summaries have not changed the source meaning remove unsupported conclusions review language for neutrality and clarity make sure generated text does not invent an institution, procedure, requirement or legal provision If a fact cannot be verified confidently, do not publish it as established fact. Do not invent fees, deadlines, requirements or eligibility rules guess the current holder of a public office present a Bill as though it is already an Act present an editorial summary as the official legal text collect government application passwords or credentials pretend to process an official government transaction endorse political parties, candidates or campaigns publish unverified allegations as fact copy promotional language from an institution uncritically use “click here” as link text use unnecessary all-capital headings use stock-photo hero banners or marketing card grids as a substitute for useful civic content describe CitizenGuide.KE as “Kenya's GOV.UK” or imply that it is an official government platform Review before publishing Before publishing or materially updating a page, check: Does the page answer a clear user need? Is the title accurate and specific? Are important facts supported by appropriate sources? Are names, dates and office holders current? Are any quoted fees or deadlines dated or qualified? title: County vs national government
snippet: Which level of government does what in Kenya — a citizen guide to devolution and the Fourth Schedule.
content: County vs national government Which level of government does what in Kenya — a citizen guide to devolution and the Fourth Schedule. Home Government County vs national County vs national government Why it matters Before 2010, most power sat at the centre. The Constitution introduced devolution so that some services and decisions happen closer to communities. Functions are mainly listed in the Fourth Schedule (distribution of functions between the national government and the county governments). Read for the full chapter text on this site. Some services involve both levels — for example health policy may be national while many public hospitals and dispensaries are run by counties. See also local and county services and health and social care . Examples of national functions These are commonly national (simplified examples — always check the Constitution and current law for the full list): foreign affairs and international trade national defence and police (national security organs) immigration, citizenship and civil registration frameworks national economic policy and monetary policy institutions courts and the national justice system primary and secondary education policy frameworks and national examinations national trunk roads and national infrastructure in assigned areas Examples of county functions Counties commonly handle: county health facilities and pharmacies early childhood education and childcare facilities county transport and county roads trade development and regulation, including markets and local licensing county planning and development agricultural implementation and some local natural resource roles county public works and firefighting services control of pollution and public nuisances at county level Who leads each level National President, Deputy President, Cabinet Secretaries, Parliament (National Assembly and Senate), and national institutions. County Governor, deputy governor, county executive committee, and the county assembly (including MCAs elected by ward). title: eCitizen explained
snippet: What eCitizen is and how digital government services work.
content: eCitizen explained What Kenya’s eCitizen platform is, what services it provides, how it relates to other government systems and how to use it safely. Home Digital government eCitizen eCitizen explained ! Warning Check that you are on the genuine eCitizen service before entering your password, one-time password (OTP), identity information or payment details. Start on the official eCitizen portal This opens the Government of Kenya eCitizen service in a new tab. CitizenGuide.KE does not receive your login details or government payments. What eCitizen is eCitizen provides a common digital entry point for many Government of Kenya services. You can sign in with an eCitizen account and access services provided by participating public institutions. Depending on the service, eCitizen may allow you to: create or use an eCitizen account apply for a government service submit information or supporting documents make an authorised payment check the status of an application receive or retrieve documents and application records The exact process depends on the public institution providing the service. Services available through eCitizen Government institutions provide many services through dedicated areas within the eCitizen platform. These include services relating to immigration, civil registration, business registration, police services and other national public functions. The services available on eCitizen can change as institutions add, move or update their digital services. A service may be added, redesigned, moved to another government system or have different requirements over time. Check the current information shown by the responsible public institution before applying. Not every government service is on eCitizen eCitizen is an important government platform, but it is not the only digital system used by public institutions in Kenya. Some institutions operate separate or specialist systems, while others may use eCitizen for only part of a process. County governments may also provide services through their own platforms. Use the system identified by the responsible public institution rather than assuming every government service must begin on eCitizen. Money and tax — including information about Kenya Revenue Authority services Driving and transport — including transport and licensing services County governments — for services administered at county level Your eCitizen account Your eCitizen account is used to access participating government services. Depending on the service and authentication method, you may be required to confirm your identity or enter a one-time password. Treat your eCitizen account as you would any other important identity or financial account. Use a strong password that is not reused elsewhere. Keep the email address and phone number associated with your account secure. Never give another person your OTP. Do not allow an unofficial agent to sign in to your account on your behalf. Check what action you are approving before entering an OTP or authorising a payment. Using eCitizen safely Open the genuine service Type the eCitizen address yourself, use a trusted bookmark, or follow a link published by the responsible public institution. Do not assume a website is genuine merely because it uses the eCitizen name, government colours or a copied logo. Do not share passwords or OTPs You may receive a genuine OTP when signing in or confirming an action. Enter it only into the genuine service you deliberately opened. Do not send an OTP to another person through a phone call, WhatsApp, SMS, email or social media. Check before paying Follow the payment instructions shown by the genuine government service and check the transaction details before authorising the payment. Be suspicious if somebody asks for a separate personal payment to guarantee approval, move an application forward or bypass the normal process. Read our scams and fake websites guidance for more information. Government payments on eCitizen Some eCitizen services allow users to pay government fees and charges electronically as part of the application process. The available payment method and amount depend on the particular service. Always check the current fee shown by the responsible government service before paying. Check the payment details carefully before authorising a transaction and keep the payment confirmation or receipt until the service has been completed. eCitizen and Digital ID Digital identity services may be used as part of Kenya's wider digital-government ecosystem to help verify the identity of people accessing online public services. Where you need to use an eCitizen Digital ID service, start from the official government service: eCitizen Digital ID Getting help with eCitizen For problems with your eCitizen account, authentication, payments or an application, use the support channels currently published by eCitizen or by the public institution responsible for the service. Contact details can change, so it is safer to use those shown on the official platform rather than relying on a phone number or email address copied from an old page or social media post. Get help on the official eCitizen website You can also find information about assisted government services through Huduma Centres . If a payment fails If money has been deducted but the application does not show the payment, do not immediately make the same payment again unless the official service tells you to do so. Keep the transaction reference, receipt or confirmation message and contact the official eCitizen support channel or the institution responsible for the application. CitizenGuide.KE cannot trace, reverse or reconcile government payments. If an application is delayed or rejected An application submitted through eCitizen is normally handled by the public institution responsible for that service. eCitizen provides the digital platform, while the responsible institution may determine whether an application meets the relevant legal or administrative requirements. Use the contact information provided for the service if you need clarification about requirements, processing times or a decision. Find a government institution CitizenGuide.KE and eCitizen CitizenGuide.KE and eCitizen serve different purposes. CitizenGuide.KE Explains institutions, public services, laws and civic processes and helps you find the appropriate official source. eCitizen A Government of Kenya digital platform through which participating public institutions provide online services. CitizenGuide.KE does not have access to your eCitizen account, application history, government payment records or documents stored in eCitizen. Service guides on CitizenGuide.KE Our service guides explain requirements and steps in plain language and, where an online application exists, direct you to the appropriate official service. Browse services Services A to Z Browse topics Information can change eCitizen services, requirements, fees and government systems can change. CitizenGuide.KE may not reflect an official change immediately. For an application, payment or deadline, check the current information shown by the responsible government service before proceeding. title: Editorial policy
snippet: How CitizenGuide.KE sources, writes, verifies and updates information about Kenyan government, public institutions and services.
content: Editorial policy How CitizenGuide.KE sources, writes, verifies and updates information about Kenyan government, public institutions and services. Home About Editorial policy Editorial policy CitizenGuide.KE is an independent civic information platform. We are not the Government of Kenya and do not replace official legal, administrative or service information. Our purpose CitizenGuide.KE helps people understand how government in Kenya works, who is responsible for what, and where to find official services and records. We organise information around citizen needs as well as public institutions. Our aim is to make complex civic information easier to find, understand and verify. We do not publish information simply because it is available. We consider whether it is relevant, verifiable, useful to the public and appropriate to include in an independent civic information service. Our editorial principles We aim to follow these principles when publishing and maintaining content: Accuracy: information should be supported by reliable sources and presented in the correct context. Primary sources first: where possible, we rely on the original legal, parliamentary, judicial or institutional record. Clarity: we explain information in plain language without changing its legal or factual meaning. Independence: editorial decisions are not made on behalf of a ministry, political party, candidate or public body. Traceability: users should be able to understand where important factual information came from. Timeliness: information that changes should be reviewed and updated when reliable new information becomes available. Correction: verified errors should be corrected rather than silently left in place. Source hierarchy We prefer primary and authoritative sources. When sources conflict, we generally give greater weight to sources higher in this hierarchy: the Constitution of Kenya and legislation as officially published Kenya Gazette notices, legal notices, official proclamations and commencement notices judgments, rulings and other primary records published by the Judiciary parliamentary records, including Acts, Bills, Hansard, committee reports and official proceedings records and publications of constitutional commissions and independent offices official publications and websites of ministries, departments, agencies and county governments structured datasets formally released by public bodies reputable secondary sources where primary material is unavailable or additional context is necessary This hierarchy is a guide rather than an automatic rule. The most appropriate source depends on the information being verified. For example, a later Gazette notice may supersede information published earlier on an institutional website. When official sources disagree Official sources are not always updated at the same time. A public institution's website may show one position while a Gazette notice, Act, court decision or later official record shows another. Where there is a material conflict, we try to: identify the most authoritative and recent source check whether one source legally supersedes another record relevant dates avoid presenting disputed information as settled fact explain the conflict where it is important for the user to know Where the correct position cannot be established confidently, we may delay publication, qualify the information or direct users to the responsible public body. Social media and secondary sources Social media can be useful for identifying announcements, but we do not normally treat a social media post on its own as authoritative evidence for legal requirements, fees, appointments or the status of public offices. Where an official institution makes an announcement through a verified or otherwise clearly authentic official account, we may use it as an initial source while seeking confirmation from a more permanent official record where appropriate. We do not treat rumours, forwarded messages, anonymous posts, campaign material or unverified screenshots as authoritative sources. News reports, academic work and civil-society publications may be used for context or to identify issues for further research, but significant factual claims are preferably checked against primary material. What we publish CitizenGuide.KE may publish or organise information including: explanations of public institutions and their mandates directories of public institutions and office holders constitutional and statutory information Acts, Bills and legislative information court and judicial information Gazette notices and other official records county government information guidance that helps users identify the appropriate official service or public institution public-service fees and requirements where reliably sourced structured public datasets with source information civic explainers on subjects such as devolution, elections, public finance and the structure of government The fact that CitizenGuide.KE includes information about an institution, person, law or public service does not imply endorsement by that institution or person. What we do not publish CitizenGuide.KE is an informational service rather than a political campaign or official transaction platform. We do not intentionally publish: party-political campaigning or candidate endorsements unverified rumours presented as fact allegations about individuals without a reliable and appropriate public-interest basis instructions intended to facilitate unlawful access to public or private systems pages designed to impersonate an official government service government payment forms or payment collection presented as an official government transaction personal information merely because it can technically be found somewhere online Public office holders and personal information Information about public office holders may be included where it is relevant to understanding a public institution, office, legal responsibility or official record. We aim to distinguish between information that is relevant to a person's public role and information relating only to their private life. We do not assume that personal information should be republished simply because it appears in a public document. Publication decisions also take account of relevance, context, accuracy and applicable data-protection obligations. For information about how we handle personal data, read our privacy policy . How we write and explain information We aim to make civic information understandable without oversimplifying or changing its meaning. Our detailed writing conventions are set out in the content style guide . In general, we aim to: lead with the user's information need use plain, direct language use short sentences where possible use active voice expand unfamiliar acronyms the first time they appear separate explanation from the wording of an official source preserve important legal terminology where replacing it would change the meaning identify dates where information may change over time show monetary amounts in Kenyan shillings and give relevant dates for fees where possible say when requirements or services vary between counties or institutions Plain-language summaries CitizenGuide.KE may provide plain-language summaries of laws, judgments, reports, institutional mandates and other official material. A summary is intended to help users understand or navigate the source. It is not a replacement for the authoritative document. Where the precise legal wording matters, users should consult the original Act, Gazette notice, judgment, regulation or other authoritative source. Links to official sources Where practical, we link to official sources so users can verify information for themselves. For example, legal material may be linked to Kenya Law (opens in a new tab) , while parliamentary information may link to the relevant official Parliament resource. An external-link symbol indicates that a link opens a website that is not part of CitizenGuide.KE. Dates, fees and information that changes Some civic information changes frequently. Examples include fees, office holders, application procedures, deadlines, tax information and election-related information. Where practical, we show the date on which information was checked, published or last updated so users can judge its currency. A figure or requirement that was correct on one date may later change. Users should confirm time-sensitive requirements with the responsible public body before relying on them for an important transaction. Updates and review We do not apply the same review frequency to every page. Information with a higher risk of becoming outdated may be reviewed more frequently. This can include: fees and charges election information tax and revenue information identity and immigration services current public office holders application requirements and deadlines Structural information, such as the constitutional functions of an arm of government, may require less frequent review unless the relevant law or institutional structure changes. There may be a delay between an official change and its appearance on CitizenGuide.KE. For a transaction or deadline, users should confirm the latest position with the responsible public body. Corrections and significant changes We correct factual errors when they are identified and can be verified. Minor typographical or formatting changes may be made without a separate correction notice. Where a correction materially changes the meaning of a page, we may provide additional context or a correction note where appropriate. Read our corrections policy to find out how to report an error. Attribution and source provenance Where appropriate, we record information about the source, publication date, official institution or document from which a data point or statement was derived. Source links can change or disappear over time. A broken external link does not necessarily mean the underlying information was originally unsourced, but we will try to replace obsolete links with current authoritative sources where practical. For information about ownership and reuse of source material and CitizenGuide.KE original content, read our copyright and content notices . Independence and political neutrality CitizenGuide.KE is independent of the Government of Kenya, county governments, political parties and election candidates. title: General elections
snippet: How general elections work and key dates for the next poll.
content: General Elections in Kenya | Elections | CitizenGuide.KE Information about Kenya's General Elections including voter registration, voting process, timelines, and legal framework. Home Elections General elections General elections in Kenya Held on the second Tuesday of August every 5 years, as required by the Constitution of Kenya. Next calendar milestone: — full IEBC timeline General elections in Kenya are run by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) . They determine who will serve as President , Members of Parliament , Senators , Governors , and County Assembly representatives . Voter registration To vote, you must be registered with IEBC and have a valid national ID card or passport. How to register as a voter Visit an IEBC registration centre Present your national ID or passport Provide biometric data (fingerprints and photograph) Confirm your polling station Receive a voter acknowledgement slip Check your voter registration status You can verify your registration through the IEBC voter verification system (opens in a new tab) . Election timelines For the , IEBC has published official milestones — public officer resignation, party primaries, nominations, campaign period (29 May–7 August 2027), election agents, and polling day — plus a full Election Operation Plan with every activity from voter registration through petitions. View key 2027 IEBC milestones Full Election Operation Plan timelines voter registration updates and verification candidate nominations by political parties IEBC clearance of candidates campaign period (regulated by law) election day (second Tuesday of August) announcement of results Election laws must be enacted or reviewed at least one year before a general election. Source: IEBC official timeline PDF . Candidates and political parties Kenya has a multi-party system. Candidates can run through registered political parties or as independents. Offices elected during general elections President Members of the National Assembly Senators County Governors Members of County Assemblies (MCAs) Eligibility requirements for candidates must be a Kenyan citizen must be a registered voter must meet IEBC clearance requirements must not have disqualifying criminal convictions See the full list of registered political parties and political coalitions . How voting works Go to your assigned polling station Present your ID or passport Complete biometric verification Receive ballot papers Vote in the secret ballot booth Place ballots in the correct boxes Have your finger marked with indelible ink to prevent double voting Presidential election results A presidential candidate must win: more than half of all valid votes cast (50% + 1) at least 25% of valid votes in at least half of all counties Results and transparency IEBC is responsible for tallying and announcing official results. Results are transmitted from polling stations to constituency and national tallying centres using statutory forms: Form 34A — polling station results Form 34B — constituency tally Form 34C — national presidential results Legal framework Elections in Kenya are governed by the Constitution of Kenya (2010) and supporting laws. Constitutional provisions Article 38 — Political rights Guarantees every citizen the right to free, fair and regular elections. Article 81 — General principles of the electoral system Requires elections to be free from violence, with fair representation and gender equity. Article 82 — Legislation on elections Directs Parliament to enact laws on voter registration, boundaries and election procedures. Article 86 — Voting Requires voting to be simple, accurate, verifiable, secure, accountable and transparent. Article 88 — IEBC Establishes the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission . Article 101 — Election of members of Parliament Sets parliamentary elections for the second Tuesday of August every 5 years. Article 136 — Election of the President Establishes presidential election timing and the 50% + 1 requirement. Articles 177 and 180 — County elections Legal basis for election of Governors and Members of County Assemblies. Acts of Parliament Elections Act (2011) Governs voter registration, candidate nominations, election procedures and dispute resolution. Administered by IEBC. Political Parties Act Regulates formation, registration, funding and internal democracy of political parties. Administered by the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP) . IEBC Act Defines the powers, structure and mandate of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission. Election Campaign Financing Act Regulates campaign spending limits and requires disclosure of political donations. Regulations and codes Electoral Code of Conduct Regulations Enforces ethical conduct during campaigns, including prohibitions on bribery, violence and hate speech. IEBC Regulations and Guidelines Operational rules covering voting procedures, tallying and result transmission. These laws form the legal foundation of Kenya's electoral system and may be amended by Parliament or interpreted by the courts. Related pages IEBC is responsible for managing elections and referenda in Kenya, and for registering voters.

title: referendums
snippet: Home Elections Elections Referendums Referendums in Kenya A referendum is a national vote where citizens decide directly on proposed changes to the Constitution. It is only required for major constitutional amendments un
content: Home Elections Elections Referendums Referendums in Kenya A referendum is a national vote where citizens decide directly on proposed changes to the Constitution. It is only required for major constitutional amendments under Article 255 of the Constitution of Kenya. Before any referendum, ensure you are registered as a voter with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) . Why referendums are held Referendums are required when proposed constitutional amendments affect key national principles. Change of sovereignty or independence of Kenya Changes to the Bill of Rights Changes to the territory of Kenya Changes to devolution structure Changes to term limits of the President Changes to independence of Judiciary or constitutional commissions Changes to parliamentary structure or national governance framework A referendum passes if it receives a simple majority (50% + 1) AND at least 20% of registered voters in at least half of the 47 counties approve it. The 2010 constitutional referendum Kenya adopted its current Constitution on 4 August 2010 after a national referendum. Choice Votes Percentage Outcome Yes (Green) 6,092,593 68.55% Passed No (Red) 2,795,059 31.45% Rejected The referendum introduced devolution, strengthened the Bill of Rights, and restructured executive authority. Other referendum initiatives Okoa Kenya Initiative (2014–2016): Failed at signature verification stage. Punguza Mizigo Bill (2019): Did not meet county approval threshold. Building Bridges Initiative (BBI 2020–2022): Declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court. How a referendum is conducted Proposal is initiated by Parliament or citizens (popular initiative) At least 1 million voter signatures are collected (if citizen-led) IEBC verifies signatures and voter registration At least 24 County Assemblies approve the proposal Parliament debates and votes on the bill IEBC issues a referendum gazette notice Citizens vote in a national ballot Legal framework Referendums in Kenya are governed by constitutional and statutory law. title: Voter registration
snippet: How to register or check your voter registration with IEBC.
content: Home Elections Elections Voter registration Voter registration in Kenya Registering as a voter allows you to take part in Kenya’s general elections, by-elections, referendums, and other democratic processes managed by the IEBC. You must be registered with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) before you can vote. Who can register Must be a Kenyan citizen (by birth or registration) Must be 18 years or older Must possess a valid National ID card or Kenyan passport Must not be registered in more than one polling station Must be of sound mind as defined by law How to register as a voter Visit the nearest registration centre Present your National ID or passport Provide biometric data (fingerprints and photo) Confirm your polling station location Receive your voter registration slip Verify your details after registration Where you can register IEBC constituency offices nationwide Mobile registration centres during voter drives Designated public institutions (schools, halls, stadiums) Special diaspora registration centres (where applicable) What you need to register Original National ID card OR valid Kenyan passport Physical presence at registration centre Personal contact details (recommended) How to check your registration status SMS verification (where available) IEBC online voter verification portal Visit your local IEBC office Always confirm your polling station before election day. Special voter categories First-time voters Citizens turning 18 should register early to avoid missing election deadlines. Students and relocated voters You may register at your current residence or home constituency. Diaspora voters Registration is done at designated Kenyan embassies and consulates where IEBC services are available. Common issues and solutions Lost details: Re-check via IEBC verification portal Wrong polling station: Request transfer at IEBC office Not found: Verify using ID number at IEBC system Legal framework Article 38 – Political Rights Article 82 – Voter registration laws Article 83 – Continuous registration IEBC Act Elections Act (2011) Register early to avoid missing verification deadlines before elections.

content: Home Government Commissions and Independent Bodies Constitutional commissions and independent bodies These institutions operate independently from the three arms of government to ensure accountability, protect public interest, and safeguard the Constitution of Kenya 2010. Often described as a quasi-fourth arm of government , these 23 bodies serve as vital checks and balances — protecting the Constitution, fighting corruption, ensuring fair elections, and safeguarding public resources. A. Constitutional Commissions Multi-member state boards established under the Constitution to protect the public interest, guide national resources, and act as a check on executive power. 13 institutions Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Manages elections, voter registration, and constituency boundaries. Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) Fights corruption and promotes integrity in public service. Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Advises on how national revenue should be shared between the national and county governments. Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) Sets and reviews pay and benefits for all public officers. Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) Promotes and protects human rights in Kenya. National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC) Promotes gender equality and inclusion for marginalised groups. Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) The Ombudsman — handles complaints about unfair treatment by government offices. snippet: Home Counties Devolution Devolution in Kenya Devolution was established under Chapter 11 of the Constitution of Kenya 2010. It decentralized statutory powers, financial resources, and administrative decision-making from
content: Home Counties Devolution Devolution in Kenya Devolution was established under Chapter 11 of the Constitution of Kenya 2010. It decentralized statutory powers, financial resources, and administrative decision-making from the national executive to 47 elected county governments. “Devolution shall ensure the participation of people in the exercise of powers of the State” — Article 174(c) of the Constitution of Kenya Objects of Devolution Article 174 of the Constitution outlines the official objectives of the decentralized structure: Promote democratic and accountable exercise of power Foster national unity by recognizing socio-cultural diversity Give powers of local self-governance to the public Recognize the right of local communities to manage their own affairs Protect and promote the interests of minority and marginalized communities Promote social and economic development and proximate public services Ensure equitable sharing of national and local fiscal resources Facilitate the decentralization of state organs and institutions Enhance institutional checks, balances, and the separation of powers Principles of Devolved Government Article 175 requires all 47 county administrative structures to operate based on: Democratic principles and structures Clear separation of powers between county executives and assemblies Institutional accountability, fiscal responsibility, and public transparency Reliable and equitable pathways for resource sharing Key Statutory Legislation The practical execution of devolution is operationalized by specific pieces of national legislation: County Governments Act (No. 17 of 2012) — Provides the legal framework for county human resources, operations, and public participation methods. Public Finance Management Act (No. 18 of 2012) — Controls county revenue allocations, tracking oversight, budget implementation, and public audit timelines. Intergovernmental Relations Act (No. 2 of 2012) — Governs dispute resolution channels and coordination frameworks between national ministries and county teams. Urban Areas and Cities Act (No. 13 of 2011) — Dictates the classification and administration criteria for towns, municipalities, and city boards. Annual Division of Revenue Act — Statutorily determines the exact vertical financial division of revenue between national and county governments. Current Implementation Status Devolution has completed over a decade of active implementation across Kenya. While local infrastructure deployment and healthcare access measurements have expanded across rural hubs, administrative challenges persist regarding local revenue collection gaps, capacity limits, and system inter-coordination.

title: The Judiciary
snippet: Courts and judicial administration in Kenya.
content: Home Government Judiciary The Judiciary The Judiciary interprets the law, protects the Constitution, and delivers justice to all Kenyans. It is independent of the Executive and the Legislature. The court system is divided into Superior Courts and Subordinate Courts. Superior Courts These courts have unlimited jurisdiction over criminal and civil matters, or specific appellate jurisdiction. Supreme Court The highest court in Kenya. It handles presidential election petitions and appeals from the Court of Appeal. Court of Appeal Hears appeals from the High Court and other courts or tribunals. High Court Unlimited original jurisdiction in criminal and civil matters. It also supervises subordinate courts. Employment and Labour Relations Court (ELRC) A specialised court that handles disputes relating to employment and labour relations. Environment and Land Court (ELC) A specialised court that handles disputes relating to land, environment, and natural resources. Subordinate Courts These courts handle the majority of cases across Kenya. Magistrates' Courts The primary courts for civil and criminal cases. They are ranked by the authority of the magistrate (Chief Magistrate, Senior Principal Magistrate, etc.). Kadhis' Courts Determine questions of Muslim law relating to personal status, marriage, divorce, or inheritance, where all parties are Muslim. Small Claims Court Provides a faster, cheaper way to resolve civil disputes involving small amounts of money. Tribunals Specialised bodies that handle specific disputes, such as the Business Premises Rent Tribunal or the Industrial Court. Leadership and administration The Judiciary is headed by the Chief Justice, who is also the President of the Supreme Court. The day-to-day administration is managed by the Chief Registrar. View the full leadership structure and directorates Judicial Service Commission (JSC) The JSC is an independent commission responsible for promoting and facilitating the independence and accountability of the judiciary. content: Home Judiciary Supreme Court Supreme Court of Kenya The apex court of the Republic of Kenya and the final interpreter of the Constitution. Established under Article 163 of the Constitution of Kenya 2010. “The Supreme Court shall be the final arbiter of the Constitution” — Article 163(3) Current Leadership (2026) Chief Justice & President of the Supreme Court Hon. Lady Justice Martha Koome, EGH Deputy Chief Justice & Vice President Hon. Lady Justice Philomena Mbete Mwilu, EGH Jurisdiction Exclusive Original Jurisdiction – Presidential election petitions Appellate Jurisdiction – Constitutional matters and issues of general public importance Advisory Jurisdiction – Gives legal opinions to the national and county governments Landmark Cases The Supreme Court has delivered several historic judgments that have shaped Kenya’s democracy. Raila Odinga & Another v IEBC & 2 Others (2017) Most famous ruling. The Court annulled the 2017 presidential election — the first time in Africa an election was nullified by a court. The Court cited massive irregularities and illegalities. Kenya National Commission on Human Rights v Attorney General (2014) Landmark decision on socio-economic rights. The Court affirmed that the Bill of Rights is justiciable and enforceable. Communications Commission of Kenya & 5 Others v Royal Media Services Ltd (2014) Defined the scope of freedom of expression and media rights in the digital age. Trusted Society of Human Rights Alliance v Attorney General (2012) One of the earliest Supreme Court cases. Strengthened the independence of the Judiciary and clarified transitional constitutional matters. Key Facts Consists of 7 Judges (Chief Justice + Deputy Chief Justice + 5 others) Decisions are binding on all other courts in Kenya Sits at the Supreme Court Building along Kenyatta Avenue, Nairobi Established in 2011 following the promulgation of the 2010 Constitution ← Back to Judiciary Overview

title: Presidency
snippet: Office of the President of the Republic of Kenya.
content: Home Government The Presidency The Presidency The President is the Head of State and Government of the Republic of Kenya. The President commands the armed forces, declares a state of emergency, and ensures that the Constitution is upheld. The Executive Office of the President supports the President in carrying out constitutional duties, coordinating government policy, and managing national security. Key offices These offices provide direct support to the President and coordinate the work of government. Chief of Staff and Head of the Public Service Oversees the day-to-day running of the Executive Office and coordinates the work of all government ministries. Secretary to the Cabinet Manages Cabinet meetings, records decisions, and ensures follow-up on government policy. State House Comptroller Manages the finances and administration of State House and official presidential functions. Deputy Chief of Staff Supports the Chief of Staff in coordinating government operations and policy delivery. Private Secretary to the President Handles the President's personal correspondence, schedule, and official communications. Statehouse Spokesperson Communicates government policy and presidential statements to the public and media. Advisory offices These offices provide specialised advice to the President on key policy areas. Office of the National Security Advisor Advises the President on national security, defence, and intelligence matters. Presidential Council of Economic Advisors Provides expert advice on economic policy, fiscal matters, and national development strategy. Office of the Women's Rights Advisor Advises on policies to promote gender equality and protect women's rights. Office of the Climate Change Advisor Coordinates the government's response to climate change and environmental protection. Constitutional bodies and councils These bodies operate under the Executive Office to coordinate national policy, security, and intergovernmental relations. Cabinet Office Coordinates the work of all government ministries and implements Cabinet decisions. National Security Council Oversees national security policy and coordinates the work of the defence, intelligence, and police services. National Intelligence Service Collects and analyses intelligence to protect Kenya from security threats at home and abroad. National Economic and Social Council Advises the government on national economic and social development policy. National and County Government Summit Brings together the President and all 47 Governors to coordinate national and county government policy. Power of Mercy Advisory Committee Advises the President on the exercise of the power of mercy, including pardons and reduction of sentences. Specialised directorates and offices These directorates carry out specialised functions on behalf of the Executive Office. President's Budget Office Coordinates the preparation of the national budget and monitors government spending. President's Economic Transformation Office Drives the implementation of the government's economic transformation agenda.
