title: How government works
snippet: Plain-language overview of Kenya’s system of government.
content: How government works How government works in Kenya under the Constitution — sovereign power, the Executive, Parliament, Judiciary, counties, commissions, elections and public accountability. Home Government How government works How government works in Kenya The Constitution starts from an important principle: sovereign power belongs to the people of Kenya. Government institutions exercise public authority on behalf of the people and within the limits of the Constitution. The Constitution is the supreme law The Constitution of Kenya 2010 is the supreme law of Kenya. All public institutions and state officers must exercise their powers consistently with it. The Constitution sets out: how sovereign power is exercised rights and fundamental freedoms national values and principles of governance the structure and powers of public institutions leadership and integrity requirements the system of devolution elections and political representation public finance independent commissions and offices Useful parts of the Constitution include: Sovereign power belongs to the people Kenya's constitutional system begins with the people rather than with the President, Parliament or any other institution. Sovereign power may be exercised directly by the people or through democratically elected representatives. Under the Constitution, that power is delegated to: Parliament and county legislative assemblies the national Executive and county executive structures the Judiciary and independent tribunals Holding a public office does not give a person unlimited authority. Every public institution can exercise only the powers given to it by the Constitution and the law. Kenya has 2 levels of government Kenya has a national government and 47 county governments . The Constitution describes the two levels as distinct and interdependent. They are expected to conduct their relations on the basis of consultation and cooperation. National government Handles functions assigned nationally by the Constitution, including areas such as defence, foreign affairs, national economic policy and other national functions. County governments Handle functions assigned to counties, including many services delivered locally. The main division of functions is set out in the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution. See which services belong to county and national government The main institutions of national government At national level, public power is distributed among the Executive, Parliament and the Judiciary. They perform different constitutional roles. This helps prevent public power from being concentrated in one institution. The Executive The national Executive includes the President, Deputy President and the rest of the Cabinet. The President is both Head of State and Head of Government. The Executive is responsible for functions such as: implementing national laws and policies directing national administration developing government policy coordinating ministries and state departments preparing national budget and policy proposals performing other executive functions assigned by law Cabinet Secretaries are responsible for ministries or areas of government assigned to them. See . The Presidency The Cabinet Ministries and public institutions Parliament Parliament is Kenya's national legislature. It consists of the National Assembly and the Senate . Parliament makes legislation, represents the people and performs oversight and financial functions given to it by the Constitution. See . National Assembly The National Assembly represents the people of constituencies and special interests provided for by the Constitution. Its functions include: participating in national law-making determining allocation of national revenue appropriating money for national government expenditure overseeing national revenue and expenditure overseeing state organs within its constitutional mandate Senate The Senate represents the counties and serves to protect the interests of counties and their governments. Its functions include: participating in law-making where Bills concern county governments determining the allocation of nationally raised revenue among counties as provided by the Constitution overseeing national revenue allocated to county governments participating in certain constitutional proceedings involving the President or Deputy President The National Assembly and Senate are both parts of Parliament, but they do not perform identical functions. Parliament overview Members of the National Assembly Senators The Judiciary Judicial authority is exercised by courts and tribunals established by or under the Constitution. The Judiciary interprets and applies the law, resolves disputes and protects the constitutional and legal rights of people appearing before the courts. Judges and judicial officers are required to exercise judicial authority independently and subject only to the Constitution and the law. See . Superior courts Supreme Court Court of Appeal High Court Employment and Labour Relations Court Environment and Land Court Subordinate courts The judicial system also includes subordinate courts established under the Constitution and legislation, including magistrates' courts and other courts or tribunals provided for by law. How the Judiciary works Crime, justice and the law Separation of powers The Executive, Legislature and Judiciary have different roles and constitutional powers. In simple terms: Executive Administers government and implements law and policy. Parliament Makes legislation, represents citizens and oversees public administration and finances within its mandate. Judiciary Interprets and applies the law and resolves disputes independently. Separation of powers does not mean that these institutions never interact. The Constitution creates checks, approvals and oversight relationships between them. County governments and devolution The Constitution established 47 county governments as part of the system of devolved government. Devolution is intended to bring government and services closer to people, promote participation, recognise diversity and support more equitable development. See . County executive Each county has an executive headed by the county governor. The county executive implements county legislation and manages the county functions assigned under the Constitution and legislation. County assembly Each county also has a county assembly made up of elected and nominated members as provided by the Constitution. A county assembly: makes county legislation approves county budgets oversees the county executive represents residents of the county County vs national government Browse county governments How devolution works Who does what? One of the most common sources of confusion is which level of government is responsible for a service. Examples of functions assigned nationally include areas such as: foreign affairs defence and national security immigration and citizenship national economic policy national transport functions County functions include many locally delivered services, such as: county health services county transport functions trade development and regulation within county functions county planning and development pre-primary education certain agriculture functions Some sectors involve responsibilities at both levels, so the precise constitutional or statutory function matters. Check county and national government responsibilities Independent commissions and offices The Constitution establishes a number of commissions and independent offices to perform specialised constitutional functions. See . Their purposes include protecting constitutionalism, democratic governance, accountability and particular areas of public administration. Examples include: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission — elections and electoral boundaries within its mandate Commission on Revenue Allocation — recommendations on sharing nationally raised revenue Public Service Commission — constitutional public-service functions Salaries and Remuneration Commission — remuneration functions for state and public officers within its mandate Kenya National Commission on Human Rights — protection and promotion of human rights The Constitution also establishes the independent offices of the Auditor-General and Controller of Budget. Browse commissions and independent offices Elections and representation Elections are one of the main ways citizens exercise sovereign power through representatives. Kenyan voters elect public representatives including: the President Members of the National Assembly county woman representatives to the National Assembly senators county governors Members of County Assembly (MCAs) The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) administers elections and performs other electoral functions given to it by the Constitution and legislation. Political rights are protected under . See also . Elections and voting Government between elections Democracy does not end after an election. Citizens can take part in government and hold institutions accountable between elections. Depending on the issue, this can include: taking part in public participation processes submitting views on Bills and budgets petitioning Parliament or a county assembly requesting information from public bodies contacting elected representatives making complaints about public services challenging unlawful government action through legal processes Find your representatives National values apply to government Article 10 of the Constitution sets out national values and principles of governance that bind state organs, state officers, public officers and other persons when applying or interpreting the Constitution, enacting or applying law, or making and implementing public policy. These include: the rule of law democracy participation of the people human dignity equity social justice inclusiveness equality human rights non-discrimination good governance integrity transparency accountability Public money and accountability Public institutions also operate within constitutional rules on taxation, budgeting, spending, borrowing, audit and revenue sharing. National and county governments prepare budgets, while institutions including Parliament, county assemblies, the Controller of Budget and Auditor-General perform different financial oversight functions. See . How public money works Checks and accountability No single institution is responsible for all government accountability. Different mechanisms include: parliamentary and county assembly oversight independent courts constitutional commissions and independent offices financial audit budget oversight public participation access to information administrative complaint procedures elections If you have a problem with a government service or public body, the correct route depends on the type of complaint. How to complain about government Who should I contact? Start with the institution responsible for the particular function or service. For example: National service Contact the responsible ministry, state department, agency or other national institution. County service Contact the relevant county department or county government. Elected representative Find the MP, senator, woman representative, governor or MCA associated with your area or issue. Complaint or oversight issue The correct oversight body depends on whether the issue involves administration, corruption, policing, human rights, elections or another specialised area. Contact government Find your representatives Complain about government A simple way to understand the system People Hold sovereign power. Constitution Sets the rules, institutions, rights and limits on public power. Executive Administers government and implements law and policy. Parliament and county assemblies Make legislation, represent the public and conduct oversight. Judiciary Resolves disputes and interprets and applies the law independently. Counties Exercise devolved functions and provide many services locally. Independent bodies Perform specialised constitutional oversight and governance functions. This page is a simplified explanation of Kenya's constitutional system. For the precise powers and duties of an institution, read the Constitution and the legislation governing that institution. title: How public money works
snippet: How public money works in Kenya — taxes, budgets, borrowing, national and county revenue sharing, spending, auditing and public participation.
content: How public money works How public money works in Kenya — taxes, budgets, borrowing, national and county revenue sharing, spending, auditing and public participation. Home Government How public money works How public money works Public money is not simply money held by a ministry or county department. Its collection, allocation, withdrawal, spending and auditing are governed by the Constitution and public finance laws. The public money cycle A simplified way to understand public finance is: Government raises revenue through taxes, charges, grants and other lawful sources. Government prepares a budget setting out expected revenue and proposed spending. Parliament or a county assembly approves spending through the budget and appropriation process. Money is withdrawn from public funds in accordance with the law. Ministries, agencies and counties spend the money on approved programmes and services. Spending is reported, examined and audited so that institutions can be held accountable. The constitutional principles governing this system are set out in . Principles of public finance Article 201 of the Constitution sets principles that apply to public finance in Kenya. They include: openness and accountability public participation in financial matters fair sharing of the burden of taxation equitable sharing of nationally raised revenue between national and county governments equitable development of the country fairness between present and future generations when public resources and borrowing are used prudent and responsible use of public money responsible financial management clear fiscal reporting Where public money comes from Government revenue comes from several sources. Taxes are important, but they are not the only source of public money. Sources can include: income tax value added tax (VAT) excise duties customs duties fees and charges for public services county own-source revenue grants investment and other non-tax income borrowing used to finance a budget deficit National taxes Under Article 209 of the Constitution, only the national government may impose: income tax value added tax customs duties and other duties on imports and exports excise tax Many national taxes are administered by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA). If you need information about your own taxes, see money and tax . County revenue Counties do not have the same taxing powers as the national government. The Constitution allows county governments to impose: property rates entertainment taxes taxes authorised for counties by an Act of Parliament charges for services they provide County revenue can therefore include items such as property rates, permit fees, parking charges, market charges and other lawful county fees, depending on the county and service. A government body cannot simply invent a tax or licensing fee. Article 210 of the Constitution requires taxes and licensing fees to be imposed, waived or varied in accordance with legislation. Where government money is kept The Constitution establishes public funds through which government revenue is managed. Consolidated Fund Money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is generally paid into the Consolidated Fund, subject to exceptions provided by law. Money cannot simply be withdrawn from the fund because a ministry wants to spend it. The withdrawal must have legal authority. County Revenue Fund Each county has a County Revenue Fund. Money raised or received by or on behalf of the county government is generally paid into that fund, subject to the Constitution and legislation. Equalisation Fund The Constitution also establishes the Equalisation Fund to support basic services in marginalised areas so that the quality of those services can be brought closer to the level generally enjoyed elsewhere in Kenya. The Constitution identifies services including water, roads, health facilities and electricity. How the national budget is made Kenya's budget is a process, not a single event on Budget Day. Work on the next financial year begins months before Parliament approves the final spending plans. The National Treasury manages the national government budget process. Budget Policy Statement An important stage is the Budget Policy Statement (BPS). It sets out broad strategic priorities and the fiscal framework for the coming financial year and the medium term. It includes information such as: the economic outlook expected revenue planned expenditure borrowing and deficit financing proposed expenditure limits indicative transfers to county governments fiscal risks and financial objectives Budget Policy Statements — National Treasury Budget estimates Ministries and other national government entities prepare detailed estimates showing how much they expect to spend and on which programmes. The Public Finance Management Act requires the national budget estimates to identify expenditure by vote and programme and to distinguish recurrent and development expenditure. National Assembly approval The national government's estimates are considered by the National Assembly. Parliamentary committees examine proposed expenditure and are required to take public views into account. Approval of budget estimates does not by itself mean every public body can immediately take money from the Treasury. Spending must also have the required legal authority. Appropriation and taxation are different Several Bills and Acts appear during a budget cycle. They do different jobs. Finance legislation Deals with revenue measures such as taxes and other fiscal proposals. It is about how government raises revenue. Appropriation Act Gives legal authority for specified public expenditure. It is about what government is authorised to spend. Division of Revenue Act Provides for the division of nationally raised revenue between the national and county levels of government for the financial year. County Allocation of Revenue Act Provides for the allocation among the 47 counties of the county governments' share of nationally raised revenue and related allocations for the financial year. How counties get a share of national revenue Revenue raised nationally is shared between the national and county levels of government. This is commonly described using two terms: Vertical sharing Deciding how nationally raised revenue is divided between the national government and the county level of government. Horizontal sharing Deciding how the county share is distributed among Kenya's 47 county governments. The Commission on Revenue Allocation The Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) makes recommendations on the basis for equitable sharing of nationally raised revenue both between the two levels of government and among county governments. CRA considers the constitutional criteria for equitable sharing, including the functions of the two levels of government, county needs, economic disparities and fiscal responsibility. Commission on Revenue Allocation The 15% constitutional minimum Article 203 of the Constitution provides that the equitable share allocated to county governments must be at least 15% of all revenue collected by the national government. For this constitutional calculation, the percentage is based on the most recent audited accounts of revenue received that have been approved by the National Assembly. The 15% figure is a minimum, not a fixed county share. The amount allocated to counties in a particular year can be higher than the constitutional minimum. How the money is divided among the 47 counties The Constitution gives the Senate the role of determining periodically the basis for sharing the county equitable share among the 47 counties, after considering CRA's recommendations and the constitutional criteria. The formula can therefore change over time. Factors used in a particular revenue-sharing basis should be checked against the current parliamentary determination rather than assumed from an older formula. Counties can receive more than the equitable share The equitable share is not necessarily the only transfer a county receives from the national level. Counties may also receive additional allocations from the national government's share of revenue, including allocations connected to particular programmes or purposes where provided for by law. They may also receive grants and other lawful financing. How county budgets work Each of Kenya's 47 county governments has its own budget process. The county treasury prepares the county's fiscal plans and budget estimates, while the county assembly considers and approves the budget. County Fiscal Strategy Paper Each county prepares a County Fiscal Strategy Paper setting out its broad priorities and financial outlook for the coming financial year and the medium term. The Public Finance Management Act requires the county treasury to seek and take into account views from the public when preparing this document. County budget estimates The county executive submits budget estimates to the county assembly. The estimates show expected revenue and planned expenditure by county entities and programmes. The county assembly considers the estimates and takes public views into account before approving the county budget. County Finance and Appropriation laws Counties also enact laws necessary to implement their budgets. A county Finance Act may provide for county revenue measures, while a County Appropriation Act authorises expenditure from the county budget. What recurrent and development spending mean Government budgets distinguish between recurrent and development expenditure. Recurrent expenditure Ongoing costs of running government and delivering services, such as salaries, operations and other recurring expenses. Development expenditure Spending associated with development programmes, projects and investment intended to create or improve public assets and services. The label "development" does not by itself tell you whether money was well spent. Actual performance still needs to be examined against what was budgeted and what was delivered. What happens when revenue is not enough A government budget can plan to spend more than the revenue expected from taxes and other ordinary sources. The difference is a budget deficit . A deficit may be financed through borrowing and other lawful financing arrangements. Public borrowing is therefore part of public finance. It can provide resources now, but the debt, interest and other obligations affect future budgets. Article 201 requires the burdens and benefits of the use of public resources and public borrowing to be shared equitably between present and future generations. A budget is not the same as actual spending This distinction is important when reading government figures. Budgeted What government planned or was authorised to spend. Released Money made available during budget implementation. Spent Expenditure actually incurred or recorded. Audited Spending and financial statements examined later through the audit process. A headline saying that KSh 10 billion was "allocated" does not necessarily mean KSh 10 billion was eventually spent or that the intended result was delivered. Who checks public spending Controller of Budget The Controller of Budget is an independent office established under Article 228 of the Constitution. The Controller oversees implementation of national and county budgets by authorising withdrawals from specified public funds. A withdrawal cannot be approved unless the Controller is satisfied that it is authorised by law. The office also publishes reports on national and county budget implementation. Office of the Controller of Budget Auditor-General The Auditor-General independently audits the accounts of national and county government institutions and other public entities that fall within the constitutional mandate. An audit looks back at how public money was accounted for and used. Audit reports can identify matters requiring explanation, correction, recovery or further scrutiny. Office of the Auditor-General Parliament and county assemblies Parliament exercises national-level budget and financial oversight through the constitutional and legislative process, including committees that examine expenditure and audit findings. County assemblies perform corresponding legislative and oversight functions over county budgets and county public finances. National Treasury and county treasuries The National Treasury manages the national public finance framework and national budget process within its legal mandate. County treasuries perform public financial management functions for their respective county governments. Controller of Budget and Auditor-General are different These offices are sometimes confused, but their roles are not the same. Controller of Budget Primarily oversees budget implementation and authorises lawful withdrawals from specified public funds. Auditor-General Audits public accounts and reports on how public resources were accounted for and used. Put simply: the Controller of Budget is closely involved during budget implementation, while the Auditor-General provides independent audit scrutiny of public accounts and spending. Supplementary budgets An approved annual budget can change during the financial year. Government may seek supplementary appropriations where additional spending or changes to previously approved allocations are legally justified. A supplementary budget does not mean the ordinary approval process disappears. Changes to public expenditure still require the constitutional and legislative authority applicable to them. Public participation in budgets Public participation is not simply a courtesy. Article 201 of the Constitution expressly includes public participation as a principle of public finance. The Public Finance Management Act also builds public participation into national and county budget processes. Opportunities may include: public budget hearings submissions to parliamentary committees county budget consultations comments on fiscal strategy documents participation through County Budget and Economic Forums Notices, deadlines and submission methods change from one budget cycle to another, so check current notices from Parliament, the National Treasury, your county government and county assembly. How to read a public budget When you see a budget figure, ask: Which financial year is this? Is the figure proposed, approved or actual? Is it recurrent or development expenditure? Which ministry, department, agency or county owns it? What programme or project is the money for? Has the money actually been released? How much has actually been spent? What was actually delivered? What did the Controller of Budget report? What did the Auditor-General find? Allocation does not mean expenditure. A budget tells you what government plans or is authorised to spend. Budget implementation and audit reports help show what happened afterwards. Where to find official public finance information National Treasury National budgets, fiscal policy, Budget Policy Statements and related documents. Commission on Revenue Allocation Revenue-sharing recommendations and information about financing county governments. Office of the Controller of Budget National and county budget implementation reports. Office of the Auditor-General Audit reports for ministries, counties, state corporations and other public entities. title: national symbols
snippet: Home Society and culture National symbols National identity and heritage National symbols of Kenya Article 9(1) of the Constitution of Kenya establishes the official national symbols. These represent the sovereignty, uni
content: Home Society and culture National symbols National identity and heritage National symbols of Kenya Article 9(1) of the Constitution of Kenya establishes the official national symbols. These represent the sovereignty, unity and shared values of the Republic. The National Flag, Emblems and Names Act (Cap. 99) protects Kenya's national symbols. It is an offence to use the Coat of Arms, Public Seal or other protected emblems for commercial purposes without written permission from the Cabinet Secretary. For this reason, this page provides textual descriptions of the symbols rather than graphic reproductions. The national flag The national flag is the most recognised symbol of Kenya. It is based on the flag of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), which led the country to independence in 1963. The flag has a ratio of 2:3 (height to width). From top to bottom, it consists of equal horizontal bands of black, white, red, white and green, with a traditional Maasai shield and two crossed spears in the centre. Meaning of the flag elements The meaning of each element on the national flag Element Meaning Black The people of Kenya Red The blood shed during the struggle for independence Green The country's natural wealth and agricultural resources White fimbriation Peace, honesty and unity Shield and spears The defence of freedom and national sovereignty ! Warning Flying the national flag on private vehicles is restricted by law to the President, Deputy President, Chief Justice, Speakers of Parliament, Cabinet Secretaries and accredited foreign diplomats. The Coat of Arms The Coat of Arms is the official state emblem of Kenya. It is used on government documents, official correspondence and state buildings. The design is described in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. The Coat of Arms contains the following elements: Two lions — two golden African lions standing on either side, holding traditional spears. They symbolise wildlife heritage and national courage. The central shield — features the national colours (black, red, green and white) with a rooster holding an axe. The rooster represents the new dawn and the spirit of hard work. Mount Kenya — the entire composition rests on a silhouette of Mount Kenya, the country's highest mountain. Agricultural produce — the foreground shows Kenya's main crops: coffee, pyrethrum, sisal, tea, maize and pineapples. The motto scroll — at the base, a scroll bears the national motto "Harambee". The national anthem Kenya's national anthem was composed in 1963 by a committee led by Graham Hyslop, G.W. Senoga Zake, Peter Kibukosya and Washington Omondi. It was first performed at the independence ceremony on 12 December 1963. The anthem has three stanzas, written in both Kiswahili and English. Stanza 1 Kiswahili Ee Mungu nguvu yetu Ilete baraka kwetu Haki iwe ngao na mlinzi Natukae na undugu Amani na uhuru Raha tupate na ustawi English O God of all creation Bless this our land and nation Justice be our shield and defender May we dwell in unity Peace and liberty Plenty be found within our borders Stanza 2 Kiswahili Amkeni ndugu zetu Tufanye sote bidii Nasi tujitoe kwa nguvu Nchi yetu ya Kenya Tunayoipenda Tuwe tayari kuilinda English Let one and all arise With hearts both strong and true Service be our earnest endeavour And our homeland of Kenya Heritage of splendour Firm may we stand to defend Stanza 3 Kiswahili Natujenge taifa letu Ee, ndio wajibu wetu Kenya istahili heshima Tuungane mikono Pamoja kazini Kila siku tuwe na shukrani English Let all with one accord In common bond united Build this our nation together And the glory of Kenya The fruit of our labour Fill every heart with thanksgiving The national motto Kenya's national motto is "Harambee" , a Kiswahili word meaning "Let us all pull together". The motto appears on the scroll at the base of the Coat of Arms. It represents the Kenyan tradition of community-based mutual assistance, where people come together to contribute resources and labour for the common good. The Harambee spirit was central to Kenya's early development, with communities raising funds to build schools, hospitals and other social facilities. The national pledge The National Pledge of Loyalty is a civic declaration recited at public assemblies, schools and official ceremonies. It affirms a citizen's commitment to the Republic of Kenya. "I pledge my loyalty to the Republic of Kenya and to the National Flag; that I will diligently serve my country with all my heart, mind and strength; and that I will maintain and defend the integrity of Kenya, against all enemies, both internal and external, so help me God." The Public Seal The Public Seal is the official stamp used by the Executive to validate important state documents, including treaties, presidential proclamations and high-level legal instruments. The seal is circular and features the graphic elements of the national Coat of Arms. It is kept in the custody of the President. Related pages

title: Open data standards and guidance
snippet: How CitizenGuide.KE publishes open data: metadata, formats, reuse, quality and what we do not publish.
content: Open data standards and guidance How CitizenGuide.KE publishes open data: metadata, formats, reuse, quality and what we do not publish. Home Open data Standards & guidance Data standards and guidance Our role What we publish Structured extracts we maintain (Supabase / Sanity) Plain-language summaries and small visual aggregates CSV/JSON downloads where an export route exists Links to official portals we do not host What we never publish as open data Contact messages, feedback or usefulness votes Page-view or search analytics User accounts or admin content Draft or unpublished editorial material Personal data beyond public office-holder directories Metadata on every dataset Each dataset page should state: Title and plain-language description Publisher (original) and compiler (CitizenGuide.KE) Temporal and geographic coverage Update frequency Licence / reuse terms Formats (CSV, JSON) when available Field dictionary and known limitations Source links where we have them Formats and access HTML summary — figures and accessible bar tables (small payloads) CSV — preferred for spreadsheets and analysis JSON — preferred for software Catalogue API — /api/data/datasets Licence and credit Open formats do not require proprietary software. Open reuse also includes commercial use; a non-commercial-only restriction would not meet the Open Definition . Source attribution and any source-specific rights remain relevant. Using the downloads and API Use the dataset’s export link with ?format=csv or ?format=json . No account or API key is needed. CSV uses UTF-8, stable field names and quoted cells. Missing values are blank; zero remains zero. JSON preserves nulls, numbers and text identifiers. Import identifier columns as text to preserve leading zeros. CSV text that could be interpreted as a spreadsheet formula is prefixed with an apostrophe; JSON preserves the original string. Ward exports accept county , constituency and q . Polling-station exports also accept ward . Use exact place names and URL-encode values. Example: Nairobi wards as JSON . Downloads fetch all matching pages, rather than the first 1,000 records. Failed downloads return an error instead of a successful partial extract. Response headers include X-Total-Count and X-Generated-At . Generation time is not the date the underlying information was verified. These are live extracts, not versioned statistical releases. Records can change while a large download is being generated. Retain your downloaded file when citing it. Quality principles Prefer stable public sources over scraping private systems Mark snapshots (for example 2022 polling stations) clearly Do not imply KNBS, IEBC or other endorsement without agreement Keep interactive pages light; put bulk data on downloads Follow open-data maturity ideas (documentation, reuse, accessibility) without claiming formal certification Versioning Large electoral or census files should be treated as dated releases. When we replace a major extract, dataset notes should say what changed. Prefer citing the temporal coverage field on the dataset page. title: Privacy policy
snippet: How CitizenGuide.KE collects, uses and protects personal data, and your rights under Kenya's data protection law.
content: Privacy policy How CitizenGuide.KE collects, uses and protects personal data, and your rights under Kenya's data protection law. Home Privacy policy Privacy policy CitizenGuide.KE is an independent civic information platform. It is not a Government of Kenya website. We are committed to handling personal data responsibly and in accordance with applicable Kenyan data protection law, including the Data Protection Act, 2019. Who is responsible for your data This privacy notice explains how the team behind CitizenGuide.KE handles your personal data. Where we determine why and how personal data is processed through CitizenGuide.KE, we act as the data controller for that information. If you have a question about how we use your personal data, you can contact us . What personal data we collect You can browse most of CitizenGuide.KE without giving us your name or contact details. Information you give us We may collect personal data when you choose to contact us, send feedback or report a correction. Depending on how you contact us, this may include: your name, if you provide it your email address or other contact details the information contained in your message any supporting information or documents you choose to provide Do not send us sensitive personal information unless it is necessary for us to deal with your request. Technical and usage information When you use CitizenGuide.KE, some technical information may be collected automatically by our systems or service providers. This may include: pages you visit and how you use the website the date and time of your visit your browser and device type technical information such as your IP address an approximate location derived from technical information information about errors, performance and security events Where possible, we use aggregated or de-identified information to understand how people use CitizenGuide.KE. Personal data in public records CitizenGuide.KE collects, organises and links information from publicly available civic and government sources. These may include the Kenya Gazette, legislation, parliamentary records, court records and publications from public bodies. Public records may contain personal data. For example, they may identify public officers, elected representatives, judicial officers, company officers or other people named in an official record. The fact that information is publicly available does not mean that we treat it as having no data protection considerations. We aim to process and present personal data from public records lawfully, fairly and in a way that is relevant to CitizenGuide.KE's civic information purpose. We may retain links between people, institutions and public records where those relationships are supported by the source material. If you believe personal data about you has been published incorrectly, attributed to the wrong person or presented without appropriate context, you can report a correction or contact us . Why we use personal data We only use personal data where we have a reason to do so and a lawful basis under applicable data protection law. Depending on the circumstances, we may use personal data to: respond to questions, feedback and correction requests operate, maintain and improve CitizenGuide.KE understand how the website is being used detect and prevent misuse, fraud or security threats organise and present information from public and civic records comply with legal and regulatory obligations Our lawful bases The lawful basis we rely on depends on why the information is being processed. This may include: consent , where you have given us permission for a particular use legitimate interests , where processing is necessary for operating, securing or improving CitizenGuide.KE and those interests are not overridden by your rights legal obligation , where we need to process information to comply with the law other lawful grounds available under Kenyan data protection law where they apply to the circumstances Cookies and analytics CitizenGuide.KE may use cookies and similar technologies that are necessary for the website to work, remember choices you make or help us understand how the website is used. We do not use personal data collected through CitizenGuide.KE for third-party behavioural advertising. Read our cookies policy for more information about the cookies and similar technologies we use and the choices available to you. Who we share personal data with We do not sell or rent your personal data. We may use trusted service providers to help us operate CitizenGuide.KE. These may include providers of: website hosting and infrastructure database and content management services website analytics email and communications services security, monitoring and error reporting Where these providers process personal data on our behalf, we take appropriate steps to require them to protect it and use it only for the purposes for which it was provided. We may also disclose personal data where required or permitted by law, including where necessary to respond to a lawful request from a court, regulator or other authorised public body. Transfers outside Kenya Some of the service providers we use may process or store information outside Kenya. Where personal data is transferred outside Kenya, we take appropriate steps to ensure that the transfer is made in accordance with applicable Kenyan data protection requirements and that the information remains appropriately protected. How long we keep personal data We keep personal data only for as long as it is reasonably necessary for the purpose for which it was collected, including where we need to retain it for legal, security, operational or record-keeping purposes. Different types of information may therefore be kept for different periods. Information contained in public records may remain available for longer where retaining the record continues to serve a lawful civic or public information purpose. How we protect personal data We use appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, alteration, disclosure, loss or destruction. No website or online service can guarantee absolute security. We review our safeguards as CitizenGuide.KE and the technologies we use develop. Your data protection rights Kenyan data protection law gives you rights over your personal data. Depending on the circumstances, you may have the right to: be informed about how your personal data is being used ask for access to personal data we hold about you ask us to correct inaccurate or misleading personal data ask for personal data to be deleted where the law allows object to certain uses of your personal data ask us to restrict certain processing request data portability where applicable withdraw consent where we rely on your consent to process personal data Some rights are subject to legal conditions and exceptions. For example, a request to delete personal data does not necessarily require the removal of information that must or may lawfully remain in an official or historical public record. To exercise a data protection right, contact us and tell us what you are requesting. We may need to verify your identity before acting on a request. Complaints If you are concerned about how CitizenGuide.KE has handled your personal data, please contact us first so that we can look into the matter. You also have the right to make a complaint to Kenya's Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC). Links to other websites CitizenGuide.KE links to government websites and other external sources. This privacy policy applies only to CitizenGuide.KE. When you follow a link to another website, that website is responsible for its own privacy practices. You should read its privacy information to understand how it handles your personal data. Changes to this policy We may update this privacy policy when CitizenGuide.KE, our data practices or applicable law changes. The latest version will always be published on this page. If we make a significant change, we may also provide a notice elsewhere on the website. Contact us If you have a question about this policy, want to exercise a data protection right or want to raise a concern about your personal data, contact CitizenGuide.KE . title: Scams and fake websites
snippet: How to spot government impersonation and fake sites.
content: Scams and fake websites How to recognise fake government websites, phishing messages and payment scams in Kenya, and what to do if you think you have been scammed. Home Help Scams and fake websites Scams and fake websites ! Warning CitizenGuide.KE will never ask for your eCitizen password, one-time password (OTP), mobile-money PIN or online-banking password. CitizenGuide.KE does not process government applications or collect government fees. When a government service must be completed elsewhere, we direct you to the relevant official service. Common warning signs Be cautious if a website, message, caller or social media account: asks for your password, OTP, mobile-money PIN or banking PIN pressures you to act immediately or threatens arrest, penalties or account closure unless you pay promises a refund, grant, bursary, job or benefit that you did not apply for asks you to pay an individual's personal mobile-money number for an official government service asks for an unofficial "facilitation" or "speed-up" payment uses a web address that closely imitates an official institution but contains extra letters, unusual spellings or an unrelated domain sends you an unexpected attachment or asks you to install an app from a link asks you to send photographs of identity documents through an unofficial channel without a clear reason Common scam patterns Fake government websites A fake website may copy the colours, logos and layout of eCitizen, KRA, NTSA, immigration, police or another public institution. The appearance of a website does not prove that it is genuine. Check the web address before entering personal information or making a payment. Phishing messages Scam SMS, email and WhatsApp messages may claim that: you have an unpaid government penalty your account will be suspended you are entitled to a tax or government refund a warrant or legal case has been issued against you you have received an unexpected government benefit The message may contain a link to a fake login or payment page. Fake government jobs Be suspicious of supposed government recruitment that requires you to make an upfront registration, interview, medical or processing payment to an individual. Fake grants, bursaries and public programmes Scam forms may promise cash transfers, fertiliser, bursaries, loans or other government benefits in exchange for a fee or personal information. Verify the programme with the responsible institution before providing information or making a payment. How to check a website Check the full web address Look at the complete domain name before signing in or paying. Criminals may use addresses that differ from the genuine website by only one letter or word. For example, do not assume a website is genuine simply because its name contains words such as eCitizen , KRA , NTSA or government . Use official starting points Many Kenyan public institutions use .go.ke domains. This can be a useful indicator, but the domain ending alone should not be your only check. Start from a website you already know belongs to the responsible institution and follow its link to the service you need. Do not trust the padlock by itself A padlock or https connection means the connection to the website is encrypted. It does not prove that the website belongs to the government or that the organisation behind it is trustworthy. Check where a payment is going Before authorising a payment, check the recipient or organisation shown by your bank or mobile-money service. If an official-looking website unexpectedly tells you to send money to a personal number, stop and verify the payment instructions independently. Official starting points on CitizenGuide.KE CitizenGuide.KE explains public services before directing you to the responsible official service. eCitizen explained — understand how to reach the official eCitizen service safely Money and tax — find tax information and official KRA services Driving and transport — find information about NTSA and transport services Huduma Centres — find information about assisted government services Contact government — find the responsible public institution Protect your passwords and one-time passwords Treat your passwords, PINs and one-time passwords as confidential. Use a different password for important accounts. Do not send passwords or OTPs through WhatsApp or SMS. Do not read an OTP to someone who calls and asks you for it. Check what you are approving before entering a mobile-money or banking PIN. Do not save passwords on a shared or public computer. Enable additional account security where the service provides it. An organisation may send you a genuine OTP when you are signing in or confirming an action. The important rule is that you should enter it only into the genuine service you deliberately opened — not give it to another person. Protect your identity documents Identity documents can be used for impersonation and other fraud. Do not send copies of your national ID, passport, certificate or other personal records simply because somebody asks for them in a message. Before sharing a document, check who is requesting it, why they need it and whether you are using the organisation's official process. If you clicked a suspicious link Clicking a suspicious link does not always mean your account has been compromised, but take extra care. Close the suspicious page. Do not enter passwords, OTPs, card details or mobile-money PINs. If a file or application downloaded unexpectedly, do not open it. Open the genuine service independently rather than returning through the suspicious message. Check the relevant account for unexpected activity. If you entered your password or OTP If you entered credentials into a website that you now suspect was fake, act quickly. Go directly to the genuine service and change the affected password. Change the password anywhere else you used the same password. Sign out of other sessions if the service provides that option. Review account activity and contact the responsible institution if you see changes you did not make. If you disclosed banking or mobile-money information, contact the financial provider through its official support channel. If you sent money Do not send any more money. Contact your bank or mobile-money provider as soon as possible using an official support channel. Keep the transaction confirmation, recipient details and any messages relating to the payment. Report the matter to the appropriate law-enforcement or cyber-security authority. Be cautious if the same person contacts you again and claims they can recover your money for another advance fee. This can be a second scam targeting people who have already lost money. Keep evidence If you need to report a scam, keep evidence where it is safe to do so. Useful information can include: the website address screenshots SMS, WhatsApp or email messages phone numbers and account names payment or transaction references the date and approximate time of the incident Do not publish sensitive evidence publicly if it contains passwords, identification numbers, bank details or other personal information. Report a cyber-security incident Kenya's National Kenya Computer Incident Response Team Coordination Centre (KE-CIRT/CC) provides a channel for reporting cyber-security incidents. Report an incident to KE-CIRT/CC (opens in a new tab) Report bribery or corruption If somebody demands a bribe or another improper payment in connection with a public service, you can report suspected corruption to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC). Report corruption to EACC (opens in a new tab) You can also read our complain about government guidance to find the appropriate complaint route. Phishing that mentions CitizenGuide.KE Someone may falsely claim to represent CitizenGuide.KE or copy our branding. CitizenGuide.KE does not process government applications, issue licences or certificates, or collect government service fees. Treat a message as suspicious if somebody claiming to represent CitizenGuide.KE asks you to: pay for a passport, ID, licence or government application send an eCitizen, KRA or other government-service password provide an OTP or mobile-money PIN send money to an individual so that a government application can be approved or accelerated If you encounter a website, message or account impersonating CitizenGuide.KE, tell us . Before you pay for a government service Before making an important payment: make sure you deliberately opened the official service check the amount against current official information check the recipient shown before authorising payment keep the official receipt or transaction confirmation stop if somebody asks for an additional unofficial payment to complete or accelerate the process Information on CitizenGuide.KE We try to link users to authoritative government sources and identify external destinations clearly. However, government web addresses, payment methods and procedures can change. For an important transaction, check the responsible institution's current information before providing sensitive information or making a payment. Read our disclaimer for more information about using CitizenGuide.KE. title: constitution and national values
snippet: Home Society and culture Constitution and national values National identity and heritage The Constitution and national values An overview of Kenya's constitutional framework, the core principles of governance, and the sh
content: Home Society and culture Constitution and national values National identity and heritage The Constitution and national values An overview of Kenya's constitutional framework, the core principles of governance, and the shared values that shape civic life. Introduction to the Constitution The Constitution of Kenya was promulgated on 27 August 2010. It is the supreme law of the Republic and binds all state organs, public officers, and citizens. The Constitution: sets up the framework for how Kenya is governed protects fundamental rights through a comprehensive Bill of Rights divides authority between the national government and 47 county governments establishes the values that hold the nation together Read the full Constitution of Kenya 2010 on this website. National values and principles of governance Article 10 of the Constitution lists the national values that bind all state organs, state officers, public entities, and citizens whenever they apply or interpret the law, or make public policy decisions. Patriotism and national unity Encourages devotion to the development, security and cultural heritage of Kenya. It prioritises shared nationhood over individual or ethnic interests. Sharing and devolution of power Prevents the concentration of absolute authority in one central body. Power and resources are shared across the 47 county governments. The rule of law Every person, regardless of rank or status, is equal before the law. No one is above the law. Democracy and participation of the people Governance must be carried out through democratically elected representatives and open public participation. Human dignity, equity and social justice All public systems must protect the inherent worth of every person, ensure fair distribution of resources, and remove barriers that disadvantage marginalised communities. Equality Every person is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law, including full and equal enjoyment of all rights and fundamental freedoms. Protection of the marginalised The interests of minority and marginalised groups must be protected and given special attention in national development. Good governance, integrity, transparency and accountability Public administration must be transparent, free from corruption, and answerable to the public. Sustainable development Development must meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. National identity and diversity The Constitution recognises Kenya's cultural diversity as the foundation of its national identity. It balances a single, shared citizenship with deep respect for different ethnic traditions and languages. Explore related topics: National symbols — the flag, Coat of Arms, anthem, motto and pledge Languages — Kiswahili as the national language, alongside English and indigenous languages Communities — population data on Kenya's ethnic communities Religion and faith — Kenya's diverse religious traditions Structure of government The Constitution divides state authority into three independent branches, plus a devolved tier of government: The Executive — the President, Deputy President and Cabinet. Executes national laws and state policy. The Legislature — the National Assembly and Senate. Makes laws and oversees public spending. The Judiciary — the courts, headed by the Chief Justice. Independent and has exclusive authority to interpret the law. Devolved government — 47 County Governments, each with a County Executive (headed by a Governor) and a County Assembly. See the full government directory for a complete list of all state institutions. Fundamental rights and freedoms Chapter 4 of the Constitution contains a comprehensive Bill of Rights. It protects individual liberties and group rights. Key rights include: Equality and freedom from discrimination — equal treatment before the law regardless of race, sex, religion, ethnicity or social origin Right to life — life begins at conception Human dignity — every person has inherent dignity and the right to have that dignity respected Freedom of expression and media — includes freedom to seek, receive and impart information Freedom of religion and conscience — no state religion; every person may worship freely Freedom of assembly and association — the right to gather peacefully and form organisations Political rights — the right to vote, stand for election and participate in political processes Economic and social rights — the right to health care, clean water, adequate housing, food, social security and education Environmental rights — the right to a clean and healthy environment Consumer rights — the right to goods and services of reasonable quality Protection for specific groups — tailored protections for children, youth, persons with disabilities, older members of society and minority communities Read the full Bill of Rights (Chapter 4) . Civic responsibilities A strong democracy depends on active civic participation. Key duties of Kenyan citizens include: Respecting the Constitution — upholding, defending and obeying the law Paying taxes — contributing national and county taxes to fund public services Democratic participation — registering to vote and taking part in elections and referendums Respecting others — tolerating diverse opinions and protecting the freedoms of fellow citizens Protecting the environment — cooperating with conservation efforts to preserve natural resources for future generations Reporting corruption — reporting abuse of power and misuse of public resources Public participation Public participation is a constitutional requirement. All law-making and public policy processes must include opportunities for citizens to contribute. Government ministries, parliamentary committees and county executives are required to: give timely notice of proposed laws and policies hold public forums and consultations consider public views before making decisions Citizens can take part through: Town hall meetings — attending county budget forums to influence local development priorities Written submissions — sending memoranda to Parliament on pending bills Citizen petitions — lodging formal petitions to Parliament to request investigations into public service delivery Public hearings — giving oral evidence at committee hearings Devolution Devolution divides government functions between the National Government and 47 County Governments. Its main goal is to bring services closer to the people and ensure fair distribution of resources. National government responsibilities include foreign policy, national defence, the judicial system, immigration, and economic planning. County government responsibilities include agriculture, county health facilities, pre-primary education, local transport, and waste management. Explore the 47 county governments . Constitutional commissions and independent offices Chapter 15 of the Constitution establishes independent commissions and offices. These bodies are free from executive control and are designed to safeguard democracy, protect human rights and ensure financial accountability. Constitutional commissions Multi-member bodies established under Article 248(2). Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) — conducts elections and manages voter registration Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) — fights corruption and promotes integrity in public office Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) — recommends how national revenue is shared between national and county governments Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) — sets and reviews pay for all public officers Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) — promotes and protects human rights National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC) — promotes gender equality and inclusion for marginalised groups Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) — the Ombudsman; handles complaints of unfair treatment by government National Land Commission (NLC) — manages public land and resolves land disputes Public Service Commission (PSC) — recruits and manages public servants Teachers Service Commission (TSC) — manages teachers in public schools Parliamentary Service Commission — manages the administration of Parliament Judicial Service Commission (JSC) — recommends judicial appointments and manages the Judiciary National Police Service Commission (NPSC) — recruits, promotes and disciplines police officers Independent offices Single-holder offices established under Article 248(3). Office of the Auditor-General — audits all government accounts and reports to Parliament Office of the Controller of Budget — approves withdrawals from public funds See the full list of constitutional commissions and independent bodies . Amending the Constitution The Constitution can be amended in two ways: Parliamentary process — under Article 256 , amendments to non-sovereign provisions require approval by both Houses of Parliament Popular initiative — under Article 257 , citizens can propose amendments through a petition signed by at least 2 million registered voters, followed by approval in a national referendum Amendments to certain key provisions (such as the supremacy of the Constitution, the territory of Kenya, and the Bill of Rights) can only be made through a referendum, as set out in Article 255 . Constitutional history Kenya's legal framework has evolved through three major constitutional phases: Key milestones in Kenya's constitutional history Year Milestone 15 December 1963 Independence Constitution — drafted at the Lancaster House Conferences. It established a regional (majimbo) system of government that was later centralised. 1964 to 2008 Centralisation and reform era — a long series of amendments changed the system of government. Kenya returned to multi-party democracy in 1991, and growing demands for reform eventually led to calls for a new constitution. 27 August 2010 The current Constitution — approved by 67% of voters in a national referendum. It introduced devolution, a modern Bill of Rights, separation of powers and the national values in Article 10. Related pages

Understanding public holidays in Kenya Public holidays in Kenya are governed by the Employment Act, 2007 and the Public Holidays Act (Cap. 110). How public holidays are declared Permanent public holidays are established in law. Additional or one-off holidays may be declared through an official Gazette Notice issued by the Cabinet Secretary responsible for Interior and National Administration. Once a holiday has been gazetted, it carries the same legal effect as any other national public holiday. Employee rights on public holidays Employees are entitled to a paid day off on public holidays. Employers cannot deduct salary because a workplace closes for a holiday. If a public holiday falls on a Sunday, the following Monday becomes a public holiday automatically. Holidays falling on Saturdays do not automatically shift unless officially gazetted. Working during a public holiday Employees working on a public holiday may receive: Double pay for hours worked, or An alternative paid day off (time off in lieu), where agreed. Religious and community holidays Some holidays, such as Diwali, may be designated specifically for members of a particular faith community. Public holiday dates may change following official Gazette Notices, moon sightings, court decisions or special national declarations by the Government of Kenya. title: languages
snippet: Home Society and culture Languages People and communities Languages of Kenya Kenya is a multilingual country with over 68 languages spoken across its communities. This page explains the constitutional status of languages
content: Home Society and culture Languages People and communities Languages of Kenya Kenya is a multilingual country with over 68 languages spoken across its communities. This page explains the constitutional status of languages, the major language families, and efforts to preserve linguistic diversity. Constitutional status of languages Article 7 of the Constitution recognises two categories of languages for official use: Constitutional classification of languages in Kenya Classification Language Role National language Kiswahili The language of national identity and cultural expression. Used to promote unity across ethnic groups. Official languages Kiswahili and English Used for government business, legislation, court proceedings, and official records. The Constitution also requires the State to promote and protect the diversity of languages among Kenyan communities, and to develop and promote the use of Kenyan Sign Language and Braille. Indigenous language families Beyond English and Kiswahili, Kenya is home to over 40 indigenous languages. These belong to three major African language families: Bantu languages The largest language group in Kenya, spoken mainly in the Western, Nyanza, Central and Coastal regions. Major Bantu languages include: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ) Luhya (Luyia) Kamba (Kĩkamba) Kisii (Ekegusii) Meru (Kĩmĩrũ) Mijikenda (nine dialects including Giriama, Digo, and Duruma) Taita (Kidawida) Nilotic languages Spoken by communities around Lake Victoria and the Rift Valley. Nilotic languages are divided into three groups: River-Lake Nilotic (Luo) — spoken by the Luo community around Lake Victoria Highlands Nilotic (Kalenjin) — includes Kipsigis, Nandi, Tugen, Pokot, Marakwet, Keiyo, Sabaot and Terik Plains Nilotic — includes Maasai (Maa), Samburu, and Turkana Cushitic languages Spoken mainly by pastoralist communities in the northern and north-eastern arid regions: Somali (Af-Soomaali) Oromo (Afaan Oromoo) Rendille Borana (Afaan Borana) Gabbra Orma Kenya also has a small number of languages from other families, including Arabic (spoken along the coast) and Hindi (spoken by the Asian community). Kenyan Sign Language and Braille The Constitution requires the State to promote the use of communication methods for people with disabilities. Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) is the primary visual language used by the deaf community in Kenya. It has its own grammar and structure, distinct from spoken or written languages. KSL interpreters are used in: national broadcasting services public courts and tribunals Parliament and county assemblies schools for the deaf Braille is the tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired Kenyans. The Kenya Institute for the Blind produces educational materials and official documents in Braille. Urban language evolution (Sheng) In multi-ethnic urban centres like Nairobi, Mombasa and Kisumu, a dynamic language hybrid called Sheng has emerged. Sheng blends Kiswahili grammar with vocabulary drawn from English, indigenous languages, and local slang. While it began as youth slang, it is now widely used in: commercial advertising popular music and entertainment public health campaigns social media and digital communication Sheng serves as a bridge across ethnic and class divides in urban Kenya, though it is not recognised as an official language. Endangered languages Several indigenous languages in Kenya are at risk of disappearing. A language is considered endangered when the younger generation no longer learns or speaks it as their first language. Languages at risk include: El Molo — spoken by fewer than 10 people around Lake Turkana. Considered critically endangered. Omotik — a Southern Nilotic language with very few remaining speakers. Yaaku (Mogogodo) — formerly spoken by the Mukogodo community in Laikipia County. Most speakers have shifted to Maasai. Suba — spoken around Lake Victoria, with speakers increasingly shifting to Luo. Assan — a Cushitic language that is nearly extinct. Language loss often occurs when communities shift to more widely spoken languages for economic or social reasons. When a language disappears, so does the unique cultural knowledge, oral traditions, and worldview it carries. Language preservation efforts Several institutions and initiatives work to preserve Kenya's linguistic heritage: Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) — develops mother-tongue education materials for early primary schools. Children are taught in their local language for the first three years of primary school. National Museums of Kenya — documents and archives indigenous languages, including recording oral histories and traditional knowledge. Universities — institutions like the University of Nairobi, Kenyatta University, and Maseno University offer degree programmes in linguistics and African languages. Community language boards — some communities have established boards to standardise orthography (writing systems) and produce dictionaries. Digital archives — projects like the Endangered Languages Project and local digital initiatives are creating online resources for minority languages. The Kiswahili Institute (Chama cha Kiswahili Tanzania) works regionally to promote Kiswahili across East Africa, including standardisation and development of new terminology. Related pages The Ministry of Education, Science and Technology oversees language policy and mother-tongue education in Kenya.

Athletes represent their countries in track, field, road and combined events. How often they take place The first championships were held in Helsinki in 1983. The event is normally held every 2 years. Nairobi will host the 2029 edition after Beijing hosts the 2027 championships. How they differ from the Olympics The World Athletics Championships are dedicated to athletics. The Olympic Games include many sports and are governed by the International Olympic Committee. Both competitions include elite international athletics, but they use separate qualification systems, schedules and organizing structures. An athlete's result at one competition does not count as a result at the other. Other international competitions The championships are different from the Diamond League , which is a season-long series of one-day meetings. They are also different from continental championships, road-running championships and age-group competitions. Nairobi competed with other candidate cities through a process assessing areas such as delivery plans, venues, financial support, audience potential and the proposed long-term benefit to athletics. title: Why Nairobi 2029 matters
snippet: Why hosting the 2029 World Athletics Championships matters for Nairobi, Kenya, East Africa and the African continent.
content: Why Nairobi 2029 matters Why hosting the 2029 World Athletics Championships matters for Nairobi, Kenya, East Africa and the African continent. Home World Athletics Championships Nairobi 2029 About the championships Why Nairobi 2029 matters Why Nairobi 2029 matters Nairobi 2029 will be the first World Athletics Championships held in Africa. The decision brings the sport's main global championship to a continent with a long and influential athletics history. For Kenya Kenya is one of the most successful nations in international distance and middle-distance running. Hosting allows spectators to experience a senior global championship in Kenya and creates a test of the country's ability to deliver a complex international event. For East Africa and Africa The championships can widen access for regional spectators, officials, volunteers, media and businesses. They may also support future African bids for major sporting events if the event is delivered safely, transparently and sustainably. Possible long-term benefits improved competition and training facilities experience for Kenyan and African event officials greater participation and interest among young people international tourism and media attention opportunities for local suppliers and workers stronger systems for staging future events Benefits are not automatic Expected benefits should not be presented as completed outcomes. Public authorities and organizers will need measurable plans for costs, procurement, accessibility, environmental impact, facility use and community benefit after the championships.
